stories.title: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in $43.9 billion all-stock deal
stories.summary: CrowdStrike will acquire Zscaler at a roughly 34% premium, targeting $1 billion of revenue synergies and $500 million of cost savings, according to its release.

facts.v: About $43.9B, based on CrowdStrike's Nov 20 close
CrowdStrike holders about 84.1%, Zscaler holders about 15.9%
About $1B revenue run-rate in 30 months; $500M cost run-rate in 18-24 months

stories.why: The largest security deal of the year joins endpoint and network security and sets a template for platform consolidation.
stories.cs: Expect integration planning, cost take-out, vendor-consolidation and security-architecture work on both sides, plus CISOs re-running their vendor strategy and contract renewals as the combined platform pushes bundled pricing.
stories.take: The numbers are the buyer's targets, not results: $500 million of cost savings is the part consultants will be asked to deliver and the part customers will feel as vendor and data-centre consolidation.
paras: CrowdStrike said on Monday 23 November 2026 that it will acquire Zscaler in an all-stock transaction that values the network-security company at about $43.9 billion, based on CrowdStrike's closing price on 20 November. According to the joint release, each Zscaler share converts into 1.135 CrowdStrike shares, worth about $260.41 on that basis and a premium of roughly 34% to Zscaler's 20 November close. Both boards approved the deal unanimously. Zscaler founder Jay Chaudhry and affiliates, who hold about 34% of Zscaler's shares, signed voting agreements.

Because the price is paid in shares, Zscaler holders will own about 15.9% of the combined company and CrowdStrike holders about 84.1%. Closing is expected in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, which falls in calendar 2027, and needs a Zscaler shareholder vote, regulatory approvals and customary conditions. CrowdStrike will file a Form S-4 containing the proxy statement and prospectus. TechCrunch reported a close around this time next year, which differs slightly from the company's own timing, so this article uses the release. The two companies run separately until then, and Chaudhry will continue to lead the Zscaler business and join the CrowdStrike board.

The companies were also reporting results the same day: CrowdStrike its fiscal third quarter and Zscaler its fiscal first quarter. They moved a joint call to 5:00 a.m. Pacific on 23 November, replacing one that had been set for 1 December. The releases point readers to the companies' investor sites for the quarterly figures, and this article does not report them.

The commercial argument is about reach and control. CrowdStrike says the combined business will have more than $10 billion of annual recurring revenue at close, of which Zscaler reported about $3.9 billion in its latest quarter, and that the deal expands its addressable market by more than $185 billion in calendar 2029. The two share more than 2,000 customers and 16 integrations, while about 8,000 Zscaler customers do not use CrowdStrike, according to the release. Zscaler says its platform protects half of the Fortune 500, operates from more than 200 locations and processes more than 750 billion transactions a day; those are company figures. CrowdStrike plans to carry Zscaler products on its single-contract Falcon Flex licence and to feed network telemetry into its Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. George Kurtz, CrowdStrike's founder and chief executive, framed the deal around securing AI and a single control plane, and Chaudhry described it as the natural evolution of the two companies' partnership, in the release.

The synergy targets are the part to watch. CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion of annualised revenue run-rate within 30 months of closing, and $500 million of annualised cost run-rate within 18 to 24 months, mainly from data-centre infrastructure, vendors and wider operations. Those are the buyer's targets, not results. The release says the deal should be significantly and immediately accretive to free cash flow per share before synergies, and accretive to revenue growth, non-GAAP operating margin and free cash flow margin within the first fiscal year after close once synergies are counted.

Outside analysts framed it competitively. Cybersecurity Dive quotes Madelein van der Hout of Forrester saying the deal fills a network gap in CrowdStrike's offer, and Shaul Eyal of TD Cowen saying it helps the company against Palo Alto Networks. In a longer Forrester note published on 24 November, principal analyst James Plouffe calls it the largest cybersecurity acquisition to date, puts Zscaler at about 11,000 customers with about 8,000 not overlapping with CrowdStrike, and notes that CrowdStrike's last three acquisitions, SGNL, Seraphic and Dreadnode, totalled about $1.2 billion, which makes this one uncharacteristically large. Cybersecurity Dive adds that CrowdStrike also agreed this month to buy Fiddler, and that the Wall Street Journal reported prices of $95 million for Dreadnode and $400 million for Fiddler; the companies did not release terms.

Forrester sees shareholder approval as a formality given Chaudhry's 34%, and regulatory risk as higher in the European Union and United Kingdom, where investment screening could add filings. It says regulators might look at bundling through Falcon Flex and at endpoint interoperability with Microsoft Defender and SentinelOne, and judges that interoperability commitments are a likelier outcome than a block. It flags integration risk too: CrowdStrike has not integrated a company this size, Zscaler's cloud raises questions about data-centre consolidation and outage risk given CrowdStrike's July 2024 outage, and ownership of Red Canary raises vendor-neutrality questions for managed-detection customers who use other endpoint tools. Forrester lists product overlaps in cloud and SaaS posture management, data security, identity and browser security, and notes that more than 20 vendors claim secure access service edge capabilities, so Netskope, Cato Networks and others may see partnerships shift. That is one analyst firm's view, not a forecast of what regulators will do.

For buyers, Forrester's advice is practical: ask for demonstrated interoperability, and use renewal talks to secure price protection and change-of-control terms. Qatalyst Partners is lead financial adviser to CrowdStrike, with J.P. Morgan and BofA Securities also advising and Davis Polk & Wardwell as legal counsel. BDT & MSD Partners is lead financial adviser to Zscaler, with Citigroup and Goldman Sachs also named and Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati as legal counsel.

What is not yet known is whether regulators will review the combination closely, how customers will respond to bundled pricing, how much of the $500 million cost target will fall on staff, and how the two architectures will be joined. The release does not state a termination fee.
unknowns: Termination fee and detailed deal protections are not stated in the release
Scope and timing of regulatory review
How many roles the $500 million cost target affects
How the Zscaler network architecture will be joined to the Falcon platform
questions: CrowdStrike is paying a 34% premium in stock and targets $500 million of cost synergies. How would you test whether that target is credible?
What would you tell a CISO who buys from both companies about renewals during the 12 to 18 months before closing?
Which integration risks are biggest when an endpoint company buys a network-security company?

stories.title: America's Car-Mart files Chapter 11 with $10 million stalking-horse bid
stories.summary: The subprime auto dealer filed in Texas with liabilities of $1 billion to $10 billion and a proposed sale of substantially all assets to Cardinal Asset Holdings, according to TheStreet and Bloomberg Law.

facts.v: U.S. Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of Texas
$10M base cash plus $13.6M for owned real estate, inventory payments and assumed liabilities
Up to $60M of new DIP loans (needs court approval)
Dealerships cut from 154 to 94 in the year to Apr 30, 2026

stories.why: A subprime auto retailer is moving to a court-run sale after shrinking its network by 40%.
stories.cs: Restructuring, DIP-financing, receivables-portfolio valuation and turnaround work for the company and its lenders, and credit-risk reviews for other subprime auto lenders and dealers.
paras: America's Car-Mart, a subprime used-car dealer and lender, filed for Chapter 11 protection in the Southern District of Texas on Tuesday 24 November 2026, according to Bloomberg Law and TheStreet. The filing lists estimated assets of $100 million to $500 million and liabilities of $1 billion to $10 billion, which are ranges, not exact figures.

TheStreet reports that the company proposes a court-supervised sale of substantially all its assets to Cardinal Asset Holdings and affiliates as a stalking-horse bidder, meaning an opening offer that other bidders can top. The consideration includes $10 million of base cash, $13.6 million for owned real estate, inventory-based payments, rollover debt and assumed liabilities. The company also seeks up to $60 million of new debtor-in-possession loans and up to $65 million of roll-up loans. Both the sale and the financing need bankruptcy court approval.

According to TheStreet, dealerships are expected to stay open, customers should keep paying on their current schedule, and service and accident protection plans are expected to continue, subject to court approval. The proposed plan would pay general unsecured claims in full, subject to approval, and give common stockholders $2.5 million from excluded assets with possible further recovery; no recovery is guaranteed. The report says Cardinal is led by executives with automotive retail and consumer finance experience, including a former Car-Mart chief executive and chairman.

The filing follows a long contraction that the company disclosed in stages. For the fiscal year ended 30 April 2026, Car-Mart reported revenue of $1.28 billion, down 7.9%, and a net loss of $139.1 million, or $16.79 per share, according to its July results release and Talk Business. Retail units fell 14.3% for the year and 27.1% in the fourth quarter, net charge-offs reached 27.6% of average receivables from 25.9%, and the allowance for credit losses stood at 25.15% of receivables. Active dealerships fell from 154 to 94, a cut of about 40%, as 42 were consolidated in the fourth quarter alone. The company's annual report carried a going-concern warning, and chief executive Douglas Campbell said at the time that it had not yet secured the financing or alternative transaction needed to resolve its liquidity constraint, according to Bloomberg Law.

The loan book showed the strain. In the year to 30 April 2026, active customers fell 6.7% to 97,696, accounts more than 30 days past due rose to 4.1% from 3.4%, and the average contract term was 49 months, according to Talk Business and the company's release. Car-Mart's chief financial officer, Jonathan Collins, left at the end of July to join another company, and a capital-markets executive took over the role, Talk Business reports.

The company described the problem as a liquidity and capital-structure issue and not a credit-quality one. At 30 April it had total debt of $722.4 million against $1.41 billion of finance receivables, and unrestricted cash of $47.0 million. A $300 million term loan closed in October 2025, and on 19 June 2026 the company agreed an amendment with those lenders that gave covenant relief and a defined window to review strategic and financing alternatives. A special committee ran that review.

The numbers worsened after the review began. In the quarter ended 31 July 2026, reported on 9 September, retail units fell 81.9% to 2,450, total revenue fell 57.3% to $145.8 million, and the net loss was $69.0 million, or $8.28 per share. Gross margin dropped to 21.8% from 36.6%, wholesale sales rose to 23.4% of sales as inventory was run down to $35.2 million, and principal receivables fell 21.4% to $1.19 billion. Net charge-offs rose to 9.5% for the quarter and unrestricted cash fell to $27.5 million. The company also booked $13.7 million of non-recurring costs, including $9.6 million of professional fees tied to the strategic review. On 4 September it extended the lender amendment's termination date to 11 September. These figures come from the company's own releases, which were partly summarised in the pages reviewed.

Not yet known are the names of the advisers, whether competing bids will appear, how the court will treat the proposed financing, and what happens to the customer loan portfolio that borrowers continue to pay into.
unknowns: Advisers and whether rival bids will emerge
Court decisions on the sale and financing
Treatment of the customer loan portfolio
questions: A subprime auto lender with a going-concern warning files Chapter 11 with a stalking-horse bidder. How would you value the loan portfolio?
What early-warning signals would you track at a subprime auto dealer before a filing?

stories.title: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after he resigned
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously restored Huang, citing US government input that his return poses no national security risk, and created a new export-control committee, according to its filing.

facts.v: Independent-director National Security and Export Control Committee
New Chief Compliance Officer to report to the nominating and governance committee
Up about 30%+ intraday Monday (press reports; not a closing price)

stories.why: A chip supplier at the centre of AI spending reversed a CEO exit within two weeks and added a governance layer.
stories.cs: Board-governance, export-control compliance and geopolitical-risk work: clients that depend on Nvidia supply will ask for continuity plans, and companies selling advanced chips abroad will review their customer screening.
paras: Nvidia's board on Monday 23 November 2026 unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately, according to the company's filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Huang resigned on 12 November, as covered earlier in this edition, so the reversal came after 11 days. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, returns to her CFO role, and Harvey C. Jones remains board chair. Euronews quotes Jones saying the board believes Huang is the right person to lead the company.

In the filing, Nvidia says the board received input from senior levels of the US government and concluded that Huang's return poses no national security risk. Engadget reports that the board met late on Sunday and voted on Monday, that Jones had said days earlier the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, and that President Donald Trump told CNBC he had influenced the decision. Euronews reports that Trump called the outcome the correct and proper decision on social media and said he had been speaking to the board directly and indirectly. Nvidia's own filing does not mention the president.

The board paired the decision with governance changes. A committee of independent directors, advised by independent counsel, is investigating reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, and Huang supports the work and will cooperate, the filing says. The board is also creating a National Security and Export Control Committee made up only of independent directors, and is hiring a chief compliance officer who will report to the nominating and corporate governance committee. The filing gives no timetable for the investigation.

The market reaction was large. Gadget Review coverage syndicated by Yahoo Finance reported Nvidia shares up about 30% to 33% in early trading, with the Nasdaq Composite up roughly 6% to 7%, the S&P 500 up roughly 5% and the Dow up about 3%. Euronews said the move put the stock on track to add more than $1 trillion of market value, possibly a first. These are intraday figures from press reports, not closing prices. The Associated Press, as quoted in the same coverage, said Nvidia had fallen nearly 23% in the week after the resignation and was trading near $167 after the surge, still below its $186 level before the controversy. The S&P 500 had lost seven sessions in a row before Monday, and Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid noted that comparable volatility shocks have historically taken several weeks to settle.

The decision sits inside a wider export-control story. The Commerce Department added Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, and six affiliates to its Entity List on the same day, covered on the Policy page. The Next Web reports that four US departments had wanted the listing for months and that Senator Pete Ricketts pressed Commerce to explain the delay; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said publicly that Commerce holds the pen. Fox Business reports that Nvidia's own website had listed Megaspeed as a preferred cloud partner, and that Nvidia placed it on its internal no-sell list in June 2025.

The Entity List rule itself, per Tech Times, adds seven entities in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, applies a presumption of denial to licence requests, and is the first new listing in 410 days. Shipments under earlier orders may proceed for 30 days, and the rule is scheduled for Federal Register publication on 25 November. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing, and a joint Commerce and Justice Department statement on 16 November announced no charges against the company, according to Tech Times. Euronews adds that Nvidia had reported better-than-expected quarterly results the week before the reinstatement.

Political scrutiny continues. Tech Times reports that Huang and Nvidia's general counsel are scheduled to appear before House committees on 1 and 2 December, and Euronews describes Huang's session as a closed, transcribed interview. Fox News also reported that California's attorney general said an investigation into whether Nvidia misled investors continues; that is the office's position as reported, and Nvidia has not been found at fault. Huang said he was honoured and would lead with humility, Euronews reports.

For clients, the lesson is about concentration. Nvidia's supply sits underneath most large AI build-outs, and a two-week leadership scare moved major indices. What remains unknown is what the independent committee will find and when it will report, how Congress will respond to the new listing and the hearings, and whether the new committee changes how Nvidia screens customers in practice.
unknowns: Findings and timing of the independent-director investigation
Outcome of the House appearances scheduled for 1 and 2 December
Whether the new committee changes customer screening in practice
questions: Nvidia reversed a CEO exit in 11 days. What should a board put in place before reinstating a leader under scrutiny?
How would you advise a company that depends on Nvidia supply to plan for leadership and export-control risk?

stories.title: Clariant and CD&R confirm talks to buy Ashland
stories.summary: Clariant said it is in talks with private equity firm CD&R about acquiring Ashland; Reuters, citing Bloomberg, put the all-cash deal at about $3.4 billion.

facts.v: Sales $1.863B; adjusted EBITDA $385M; net debt $891M (company, Nov 3)

stories.why: A specialty-chemicals combination backed by private equity would trigger integration and portfolio work.
stories.cs: Due diligence, synergy sizing and portfolio-review work for the bidders, separation and carve-out planning if assets are sold on, and defence and strategic-alternatives work for Ashland's board.
paras: Clariant confirmed on Monday 23 November 2026 that it is in discussions about a possible acquisition of Ashland in partnership with private equity firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice (CD&R). In an ad hoc announcement from Muttenz, Switzerland, the company said it was responding to market speculation. It disclosed no price or terms and said there is no certainty that a transaction will be agreed or completed, adding that it will make a further announcement if and when appropriate.

Reuters reported that Bloomberg News had said on Sunday that the two were negotiating an all-cash deal, and gave a value of about $3.39 billion, close to Ashland's recent trading price. Ashland's market capitalisation is $3.32 billion according to LSEG data cited by Reuters, and its shares rose about 1% in extended trading. The market value has moved around: Personal Care Insights cited about $3.5 billion in August, and Mergermarket's Activist Monitor put it near $3.14 billion in October at a share price of about $68.76.

The background is an activist-driven sale process. Personal Care Insights reported in August, citing Bloomberg, that Ashland was exploring a sale after months of activist pressure and was talking to strategic and financial buyers, with Citigroup and Lazard advising. Ancora Holdings, which holds about 4.24% according to Mergermarket, went public in June pushing for a sale, and Cruiser Capital Advisors, with a smaller stake, joined it. Both reportedly threatened proxy fights if there was no progress by the September director-nomination deadline. At the end of July Ashland reached a cooperation agreement with Ancora that added two directors and created a capital-allocation advisory committee.

Mergermarket reported on 5 October, citing three sources, that initial bids were collected on 2 October, and, citing two sources, that CD&R had teamed with Clariant. Those sources said Clariant alone would face antitrust issues because the businesses overlap in personal care, which would explain the private equity partner. Apollo and Carlyle were also named as interested, with Advent and Standard Industries, a roughly 9.9% holder, mentioned in earlier Bloomberg coverage. None of the parties commented in those reports, and these are source-based accounts, not confirmed facts. Mergermarket also noted that Ashland is described as a reluctant seller and that sponsors might struggle to pay a premium of more than 10% to 15%.

On valuation, Mergermarket reports that Ancora's June presentation set a base case of 11.5 times estimated fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA, or about $76.47 a share, and a bull case of 13.8 times, or about $96. The shares closed near $68.76 in early October. Ashland reported fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $385 million, and its release credits its Life Sciences segment with a record quarterly margin and says Specialty Additives was held back by plant productivity. Whether a deal near the reported $3.39 billion would satisfy those holders is not known.

Ashland's own numbers show what a buyer would be underwriting. For the fiscal year ended 30 September 2026, reported on 3 November, sales were $1.863 billion, up 2%, and adjusted EBITDA was $385 million, down from $401 million, a margin of 20.7%. Fourth-quarter sales were $498 million and adjusted EBITDA $121 million. Life Sciences posted a 35.6% segment margin in the quarter, Personal Care sales rose 8%, and Specialty Additives EBITDA fell 31% on lower productivity at its Hopewell plant. Year-end net debt was $891 million, a leverage ratio of 2.3 times. For fiscal 2027 the company guided to sales of $1.905 billion to $1.975 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $405 million to $435 million. The release does not mention a sale process.

Clariant is itself under margin pressure. Its third-quarter local-currency sales rose 5.6% to CHF 968.8 million, but EBITDA margin before exceptionals fell to 15.6% from 17.9% as raw materials rose 12%, energy 9% and logistics 23.7%, according to Indian Chemical News. It reported CHF 79 million of run-rate savings against a CHF 90 million target for 2026, and kept its guidance for a margin of about 18%. For scale, Clariant's release states 10,281 employees and CHF 3.915 billion of sales in 2025.

The unknowns are the structure of the Clariant and CD&R partnership, which assets each would own, the price, whether rival bidders remain, and how competition authorities would view the personal-care overlap.
unknowns: Price, structure and the split of assets between Clariant and CD&R
Whether other private equity bidders remain in the process
Antitrust view of the personal-care overlap and timing
questions: A strategic buyer partners with private equity to bid for a listed chemicals company. What are the main reasons for that structure?
How would you size synergies for a specialty-chemicals combination before any deal terms are public?

sources.src: Reuters via Global Banking & Finance Review

stories.title: EY Canada puts $80 million into AI, quantum and future-of-work bets
stories.summary: EY Canada says it invested $80 million in AI innovation, future-of-work programmes and Canadian 'moonshot' ideas, including an on-site quantum computer, according to Consulting.ca citing its 2026 Impact Report.
stories.why: A Big Four firm is publicly betting on AI and quantum capacity in Canada.
stories.cs: Signals where a Big Four firm is spending to sell AI and quantum-readiness work to Canadian clients; buyers can expect pilots and joint-innovation offers, and rivals face pressure to match the investment story.
paras: EY Canada has invested $80 million in AI innovation, future-of-work programmes and what it calls Canadian moonshot ideas, according to Consulting.ca on 20 November 2026, which cites the firm's 2026 Impact Report. The spend includes an on-site quantum computer at its applied innovation centre.

The report also gives people figures: employees logged 450,000 learning hours last year, about 50 each, and more than 4,100 volunteers gave time to projects that reached 3.1 million people, including an 'AI for Good' programme. EY Canada became a sustaining supporter of the First Nations Major Projects Coalition over the year. Consulting.ca puts the firm at more than 8,300 people across audit, tax and consulting.

Alycia Calvert, EY Canada's chair and chief executive, is quoted saying Canada has no shortage of ambition. Chief technology officer Biren Agnihotri describes pairing experimentation with skills and confidence. The coverage does not say over what period the $80 million was spent, how it splits between AI, quantum and other programmes, or what revenue it is meant to support.

For the market, the notable point is the on-site quantum hardware: few Canadian advisers publicise it. Whether clients pay for quantum-readiness work, rather than treating it as a showcase, is not yet visible in the reporting.
unknowns: Time period and split of the $80 million
Revenue or client-work targets tied to the spend
The Impact Report was not linked, so figures are as relayed by Consulting.ca
questions: A Big Four firm tells you it has put $80 million into AI and quantum: how would you test whether that translates into capability a client should pay for?
Which Canadian clients would actually need quantum-readiness advice today?
stories.take: Treat the headline as a marketing number until EY says what it bought; the quantum computer is the one concrete asset.

stories.title: Deloitte takes over Valterra Platinum's finance, HR and payroll in BPO deal
stories.summary: Valterra Platinum, formerly Anglo American Platinum, has signed an outsourcing agreement under which Deloitte South Africa runs its finance, HR and payroll functions; 130+ staff transfer, according to Consultancy.co.za.
stories.why: Spin-offs create demand for outsourced back-office services.
stories.cs: Outsourcing and transition work for miners separating from a parent; shows Big Four firms pushing operate services beyond advice, with Deloitte targeting 30%+ of revenue from outsourcing.
paras: Valterra Platinum, the Johannesburg-based miner formerly known as Anglo American Platinum, has signed a business process outsourcing agreement with Deloitte, according to Consultancy.co.za on 20 November 2026. Deloitte will take over corporate support functions including finance, HR and payroll through its Finance and HR Operate practice.

More than 130 Valterra employees are moving to Deloitte's South African operations, the article says, and the appointment followed a competitive process. Valterra became an independent company in 2025.

Ruwayda Redfearn, chief executive of Deloitte's Africa business unit, is quoted saying the deal advances its ambition to scale outsourcing; the article cites a goal of more than 30% of revenue from outsource services. Valterra chief executive Craig Miller calls it an important step.

Contract value, length and expected savings were not reported. The pattern matters beyond mining: newly independent companies often outsource back-office work rather than build it, and advisers with operate arms are positioned to win it.
unknowns: Contract value and term
Expected cost savings
No company press release was linked
questions: A newly independent miner asks whether to outsource finance, HR and payroll: what would you weigh?
What risks come with transferring 130 staff to an adviser-run operate model?

stories.title: Teneo hires Roland Berger's nuclear lead Mike Granowski for energy practice
stories.summary: Teneo has hired Mike Granowski, a seven-year Roland Berger partner and its global nuclear technology lead, as senior managing director in energy and infrastructure, based in Chicago, according to Consulting.us.

facts.v: Senior managing director, energy and infrastructure

stories.why: Senior nuclear talent is moving between advisers.
stories.cs: Shows demand for nuclear and power-sector advice and the talent race for it; utilities and developers get another adviser with nuclear depth.
paras: Teneo has hired Mike Granowski as a senior managing director in its energy and infrastructure practice, according to Consulting.us on 20 November 2026. He will be based in Chicago and support clients in nuclear energy and the broader power and gas sector.

Granowski has more than 25 years of consulting experience. He comes from Roland Berger, where he spent seven years as a partner, global nuclear technology lead and North American energy and utilities platform lead. Earlier roles included Enovation Partners, Bridge Strategy Group and Navigant, and he began as a nuclear engineer at Commonwealth Edison.
Dan Gabaldon, Teneo's vice chairman for management consulting and head of energy, welcomed the hire. Consulting.us puts Teneo at more than 1,800 people in over 50 offices.
The article does not say what client work the hire is meant to win or whether others from Roland Berger are following.
unknowns: Whether a team follows him
Client targets for the nuclear build-out
questions: Why would a consultancy build a nuclear practice now?
What does a senior-partner lateral hire signal about demand?

stories.title: KPMG hires two Deloitte tax partners and team in East Africa
stories.summary: KPMG East Africa has added Deloitte partners Fred Omondi and Fredrick Kimotho and associate director Kennedy Okoyo, plus others, to its Kenya tax practice, according to Consultancy.africa.
stories.why: Team lifts are reshaping East African tax advisory.
stories.cs: Tax talent moves signal where indirect-tax and policy advisory demand sits in Kenya; clients should expect continuity checks as teams change firms.
paras: KPMG has strengthened its East Africa tax advisory practice with hires from Deloitte, according to Consultancy.africa on 20 November 2026. On 11 November it announced partners Fred Omondi and Fredrick Kimotho and associate director Kennedy Okoyo; it later confirmed Patrick Chege as associate director.

The article cites The Kenya Times as reporting that at least six more professionals moved from Deloitte to KPMG. All hires are based in Kenya. KPMG East Africa has more than 1,000 professionals and 45 partners across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda, per the report.

Omondi has 23 years of experience and previously worked at the Kenya Revenue Authority; Kimotho has 12-plus years in tax advisory and policy; Okoyo has 12-plus years in indirect tax; Chege spent about 25 years at the Kenya Revenue Authority. KPMG said the appointments strengthen its ability to support complex client engagements.
Deloitte's response and the number of clients moving were not reported.

Client moves

How should a company reassess adviser independence after a team move?

stories.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, valuing it near $1.5 trillion
stories.summary: Anthropic priced its Nasdaq IPO at $83, above the $70–78 range, selling 980 million shares for about $81 billion, according to AP. Trading under ANT is due to begin Thursday.
stories.why: The largest IPO on record, per AP, resets what a listed AI lab costs to fund and to buy from.
stories.cs: IPO-readiness, investor-relations and controls work for AI-era issuers; compute-commitment and capital-allocation modelling for lenders and suppliers; vendor-risk reviews at enterprises that buy from a newly public AI supplier.
paras: Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday 18 November 2026, above the $70 to $78 range it set when it launched its roadshow on 10 November, according to an Associated Press report carried by PBS NewsHour. The shares are due to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

AP reports that 980 million Class A shares are being sold: 956,351,354 by the company and 23,648,646 by selling stockholders. The original plan, in Anthropic's own launch announcement, was 825 million shares. AP puts total proceeds at about $81 billion and the implied valuation at $1.5 trillion, and says that makes it the largest IPO on record, ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion in June. AP does not say whether the $81 billion is gross or net of fees.

The article also cites two figures from the offering documents that matter to advisers: $6.2 billion of debt, and about $900 billion of committed compute and infrastructure spending, of which about $70 billion falls in the next 12 months. Both are as reported by AP; we have not read the prospectus itself.

Anthropic's roadshow announcement, which we read earlier this month, also described a concurrent private placement of $26 billion to strategic partners at the IPO price. A market wrap on Yahoo Finance said seven technology companies had agreed to buy that block. We could not confirm the partner list or final size of the placement in a primary document, so it is not treated as settled here.

For consultants the story is less the headline number than the commitments behind it. A buyer with $900 billion of committed spending, and a valuation that depends on it being filled, shapes the demand for data-centre, power and chip supply chains, and for the advisory work that sits around them. For listed-company clients, the pricing above range is a data point on appetite for AI exposure, but a first-day move says little about durability.
Disclosure: The Consultant Times' automated editor is built on Anthropic's Claude.

stories.title: Three in four Canadian AI leaders fear falling behind, IBM survey finds
stories.hl: Canadian AI leaders fear falling behind
stories.summary: An IBM and Oxford Economics survey says 75% of Canadian senior AI leaders think their firms risk falling behind, with governance and weak scaling of pilots the main brakes, according to Consulting.ca.

facts.k: Canadian leaders fearing they fall behind
Governance, risk and compliance cited as delay

stories.why: Pilots are plentiful; scaling and governance are where advisers are being asked to help.
stories.cs: AI governance and risk operating models, pilot-to-production scaling programmes and decision-rights redesign for Canadian enterprises; a ready client opener for IBM Canada, Big Four and boutique AI practices.
paras: Three-quarters of senior AI leaders in Canada say their organisations risk falling behind competitors at their current pace, according to Consulting.ca on 19 November 2026, reporting research by IBM and Oxford Economics. The survey covered 1,667 chief AI officers and equivalent leaders across 33 geographies and was fielded from April to June 2026.

The Canadian findings point to organisational friction more than technology. Only 15% of Canadian respondents say AI leaders hold full authority over AI investment decisions, against 18% globally. Seventy per cent say their organisations do not quickly shift decisions and resources when performance measurement shows an opportunity, and 73% say governance, risk and compliance considerations delay action.

Scaling is the recurring sticking point: 72% say transformation stalls when successful pilots are scaled, 66% cite embedding AI in core workflows, and 64% cite turning strategy into execution. At the same time, 42% report that AI agents already start and carry out actions on their own across workflows. Matthew Wetmore of IBM Canada said successful pilots alone will not deliver transformation.
unknowns: How many of the 1,667 respondents are Canadian
Margin of error and whether the full report is public

stories.title: Oliver Wyman to buy 1,200-person Synpulse in its largest deal
stories.summary: Oliver Wyman has agreed to acquire Synpulse, a financial services consultancy of about 1,200 people, which Consultancy.eu calls its largest acquisition. Terms are undisclosed; closing is expected in early 2027.

facts.v: 7,000+ in 70+ offices; above 8,000 combined, per Consultancy.eu

stories.why: A strategy firm is buying implementation capacity in financial services, the clearest sign yet that advice and delivery are merging.
stories.cs: Integration, brand and talent-retention work for the combined firm; for banks and insurers, a new option for strategy-to-build programmes and a vendor-landscape check on who now owns delivery.
paras: Oliver Wyman, the management consultancy in the Marsh McLennan group, has agreed to acquire Synpulse, a financial services consultancy with about 1,200 professionals across Europe, Asia and North America, according to Consultancy.eu on 19 November 2026. The publication describes it as the largest acquisition in Oliver Wyman's history. No price or deal terms were disclosed, and the transaction is expected to close in early 2027.

Synpulse was founded in 1996 and sells consulting and technology services: enterprise systems modernisation, digital product development and AI solution implementation. It also runs a technology division, Synpulse8, which works with more than 100 technology partners. The firm is co-headquartered in Switzerland and Singapore, with about 550 staff in each, and has roughly 100 people in the United States and Canada, per Consultancy.eu.

The deal is Oliver Wyman's second acquisition this year, after the US restructuring firm CR3 Partners. Consultancy.eu puts Oliver Wyman at more than 7,000 staff in over 70 offices, which would pass 8,000 people once Synpulse is included. Synpulse is to keep its brand and leadership team, and the article gives no long-term integration plan. Ted Moynihan, Oliver Wyman's chief executive, and Konrad Niggli and Yves Roesti, Synpulse's co-chief executives, are quoted in the announcement coverage.

For readers in consulting, the logic is visible in the target's profile. Strategy firms have long sold the plan and left the build to systems integrators; a 1,200-person firm that modernises banking systems and implements AI gives Oliver Wyman a delivery arm inside its core sector. For clients, it means one provider can now be asked to carry a programme from target-state design to implementation, and procurement teams will want to know how independence is handled where the same group advises and builds.

What is not yet known is the price, how Synpulse's Asian and Swiss client base overlaps with Oliver Wyman's, and whether other partnerships held by Synpulse8 survive intact. We have read the Consultancy.eu report only, not a company release.

paras: Publicis Sapient and Ping Identity have formed a global partnership to help large organisations replace outdated identity systems and prepare for AI agents, according to Consultancy.uk on 19 November 2026. Identity systems are the technology that decides who, or what, can access applications, data and sensitive systems.

The offer combines Publicis Sapient's digital transformation, AI and software engineering work with Ping's identity management and security products. Publicis Sapient says it will use its Sapient Slingshot platform, which it describes as AI-powered software development and modernisation, to automate parts of the job: analysing existing systems, configuring new solutions and testing integrations.

A central claim is that organisations will need to give AI agents their own identities and control which applications, tools and data each can reach. Alex Laurie of Ping Identity is quoted as saying AI agents are becoming a new class of digital identity inside the enterprise. Pinak Kiran Vedalankar, group vice president for technology at Publicis Sapient, framed the aim as accelerating identity modernisation.

That figure is the companies' claim as reported, not independently checked.

Deal terms and the number of clients lined up were not disclosed. For consultants, the practical read is that agent governance is turning into a billable identity workstream, and that vendors and integrators are pairing up to sell it as a migration project.

stories.pre: Palo Alto Networks buys Applied Compute for
stories.summary: Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy AI start-up Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion and raised its full-year revenue outlook, as quarterly revenue rose 39%.
stories.why: A cybersecurity leader pays up for post-training and inference tooling, tying AI security to the model stack.
stories.cs: Post-merger integration and AI-platform strategy work; security-architecture reviews for clients running mixed open and closed models; valuation and deal-structure support for AI start-up M&A.
paras: Palo Alto Networks said on 18 November 2026 that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Applied Compute, an AI start-up. stories.title: Target's Q3 sales rise 7.1%, helped by $301M tariff refund
stories.summary: Target reported third-quarter sales of $27.07 billion, up 7.1%, with comparable sales up 5.6%. A $301 million tariff refund added $0.50 a share, and the company raised its full-year sales outlook.
stories.why: A retailer's profit jump is part refund, part trading; the refund is a one-off that clients must strip out.
stories.cs: Tariff-refund recovery and customs-compliance work for importers; margin-bridge and earnings-quality analysis for retail finance teams; capex planning as Target guides to $5–6B in 2027.
paras: Target reported third-quarter results on 18 November 2026 for the quarter ended 31 October. According to the company's earnings release, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, net sales were $27,067 million, up 7.1% from $25,270 million a year earlier. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, with stores up 4.6% and digital up 9.8%, and comparable traffic rose 5.0%.

The profit lines are flattered by a one-off. Target recognised a $301 million pretax benefit from refunds of tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, worth $0.50 a share. Reported diluted earnings per share were $2.65 against $1.51 a year earlier. Excluding the refund, the company says GAAP EPS would have risen 42% and adjusted EPS 21%. Operating income was $1,672 million, a 6.2% margin, against $948 million, or 3.8%, a year ago, and gross margin was 30.5% against 28.2%.

On the outlook, Target now expects full-year 2026 net sales growth in a range around 6%, one point higher than its prior range, and full-year EPS of $10.65 to $11.40, which includes about $2.14 a share of tariff-refund benefits recognised so far. Guidance excludes any future refunds. The company also set 2027 capital spending at $5 billion to $6 billion. Chief executive Michael Fiddelke said results reflect progress against strategic priorities. Month-to-date November sales are in line with guidance and accelerating from October, the company says.

The release does not state the prior guidance for operating margin or EPS, so the size of the change in those lines is unknown from this document. A market wrap on Yahoo Finance reported Target shares up about 4% on the day.

The lesson for clients is earnings quality. A large share of this quarter's profit growth is a tariff refund that will not repeat, and importers across retail may be owed similar money, which creates recovery and compliance work alongside the usual margin and capex planning.

How much of the remaining refund pool Target expects to recover
Detail behind the $5–6B 2027 capex plan

stories.title: Nvidia posts $115.8B quarter and guides to $130B, minus China
stories.summary: Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8B, up 103%, and guided next quarter to $130B with no China data-centre compute, in its first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.
stories.why: The biggest supplier of AI hardware is growing faster and guiding higher, but does so under an interim CEO and with China excluded from its outlook.
stories.cs: Data-centre, power and financing programmes, plus CEO-succession, continuity and export-control scenario work at Nvidia customers and suppliers.
paras: Nvidia reported record results for its third fiscal quarter of 2027 on 17 November 2026, a quarter ended 25 October. According to the company's release, revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and 20% from the previous quarter. Data Center revenue, the segment that sells the accelerators and systems behind AI build-outs, was $107.6 billion, up 110% year on year. CBS News, citing FactSet, reported that Wall Street had expected revenue of nearly $109 billion.

Profitability was equally striking. Nvidia reports GAAP gross margin of 74.8% and GAAP operating income of $77.5 billion. GAAP net income was $65.3 billion, or $2.70 a diluted share. On those reported numbers, net income was about 56% of revenue (our computed figure), an unusually high ratio for a company that sells hardware at this scale.

The outlook is the part clients will study. For the fourth quarter, which Nvidia says contains an extra week, it guides to revenue of $130.0 billion, plus or minus 3%, with gross margin of 71.0% to 72.0%. The company says that guidance assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China. Gross margin is therefore guided below the third-quarter level, a point the release does not explain. Nvidia also reports returning $28.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter and says about $227.3 billion remains under its repurchase authorisation, after the board added $150 billion in September. The next quarterly dividend is $0.25 a share.

This was also Nvidia's first earnings report since a change at the top. In a filing dated 12 November, the company said Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and director, effective immediately. The filing gives no reason. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is interim CEO while keeping the CFO role, Harvey C. Jones has been appointed the board's first chair, and the board has begun a search that will consider internal and external candidates. Press outlets have reported on the circumstances; because they concern an individual's personal conduct and the company has not addressed them in its filings, we do not repeat them here. CBS reports, citing an unnamed source, that the board is against reinstating Huang; Nvidia has not said so on the record in the documents we reviewed.

Kress, quoted in the release, said the company's momentum is real and that its new Vera Rubin platform is off to an explosive start. CBS reported shares up almost 3% after hours, to $159.60. It also reported that the board formed a committee to oversee export-control compliance and that questions have been raised about whether advanced chips reached China in breach of rules; CBS does not say Nvidia is accused of any violation.

For consultants the numbers point in several directions. First, capital intensity: a $130 billion quarterly run-rate means customers' data-centre, power and cooling programmes are being sized in the tens of billions, and the advisory work that follows is site selection, financing structures, grid connection and supply-chain assurance. Second, concentration and governance: a company this central to AI supply chains now has an interim CEO who is also CFO, so boards and procurement teams at its largest customers will ask about continuity, key-person risk and contract terms. Third, trade policy: guidance that excludes China compute revenue shows how much planning now depends on export rules, and clients with exposure will want scenario work rather than a single forecast.

Context helps here. Nvidia's Data Center segment is now more than 90% of revenue on the company's own figures ($107.6 billion of $115.8 billion, our computed share of about 93%), so the group's results are in effect a read on AI infrastructure spending across hyperscalers, sovereign programmes and enterprises. Guidance of $130 billion for a quarter with an extra week implies further growth, but the release does not break down how much of the step-up comes from the additional week, which is why we list it as unknown. Analysts and clients will look for the company's quarterly report and call commentary for customer concentration, supply constraints and the pace of the Vera Rubin ramp.

Leadership continuity is the other thread. The 12 November filing describes an orderly structure on paper: an interim chief executive with 13 years at the company, a newly created independent board chair, and a stated search covering internal and external candidates. What it does not say is how long the search will take, which is the practical question for customers signing multi-year supply and capacity agreements.

Several things remain unknown: who the permanent CEO will be and when, why gross margin is guided down, how much of the Q4 guide is the extra week, and how customers' spending plans hold up if financing conditions tighten. We will update this item as the company files its quarterly report and as further sourced reporting appears.
unknowns: Who the permanent CEO will be and when
Why gross margin is guided below Q3
How much of the Q4 guide comes from the extra week
Whether the reported export-control questions lead to any action
questions: A client plans a $5B AI data-centre build with Nvidia as sole supplier; how do you assess supplier risk during a CEO transition?
stories.take: The numbers say Nvidia's business is in excellent shape; the open question is whether a company this central can run on an interim chief executive who is also its CFO. Clients with large Nvidia commitments should ask about continuity and contract terms now, not after the permanent CEO is named.

stories.title: Home Depot promotes CFO Richard McPhail to CEO
stories.summary: Home Depot named CFO Richard McPhail chief executive from 23 November, with Ted Decker staying as chair, on the day it reported third-quarter results.
stories.why: The nation's largest home-improvement retailer hands all three top roles to long-serving insiders.
stories.cs: CFO-office transition, investor-messaging and operating-model work at large retailers; housing-cycle scenario planning for suppliers.
paras: Home Depot said on 17 November 2026 that chief financial officer Richard McPhail will become chief executive officer, effective 23 November, succeeding Ted Decker. According to the company's release, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, McPhail, who joined Home Depot in 2005 and has been CFO since September 2019, will also be elected to the board. Decker will step down as president and CEO and continue as chair of the board.

The release names two further changes on the same date. Ann-Marie Campbell, described as a 41-year veteran of the company, becomes president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi, a 13-year veteran who was most recently executive vice president of interconnected retail, becomes executive vice president and CFO. In effect the top three roles all pass to long-serving insiders.

Asked about the reason, the company pointed to succession planning. The Atlanta Journal-Constitution quotes a spokesperson calling the change part of normal and ongoing succession planning, and WSB-TV quotes independent lead director Greg Brenneman referring to the board's ongoing, active succession planning. In the release, Decker says he looks forward to supporting the new team during the transition.

The announcement came on the morning Home Depot reported third-quarter results. WSB-TV reports that sales rose about $2 billion, almost 5%, from the same period in 2025, and quotes McPhail saying the quarter exceeded the company's expectations. Neither the release nor the two press reports we read gives earnings per share, comparable sales or guidance, so we do not report them here.

For advisers, a CFO-to-CEO promotion at a $100-billion-plus retailer tends to signal continuity in strategy and capital allocation rather than a reset. It also opens a sequence of work: the new CFO's finance organisation, the operating committee under a new COO, and any change in how the company talks to investors about housing-market sensitivity, professional customers and its acquisition-led supply-chain strategy. These are our readings of the structure, not company statements.

What we do not yet know: whether strategy, capital-return policy or the company's financial targets will change under McPhail; how investors reacted, since none of the sources we read reports a share-price move; and what Decker's role as chair will involve in practice.
unknowns: Whether strategy or capital-return policy will change under McPhail

stories.title: JPMorgan names Bregje de Best to succeed CFO Jeremy Barnum

stories.why: A staged succession at the largest US bank, announced alongside continuing speculation about CEO succession.
stories.cs: Finance-function and investor-relations work: succession planning, CFO-office transitions and capital-messaging prep at large banks.
paras: JPMorgan Chase said on 17 November 2026 that Bregje de Best, currently chief financial officer of its Corporate & Investment Bank, will succeed Jeremy Barnum as the firm's chief financial officer. According to the company's release, the handover happens after the first-quarter 2027 financial reporting, at which point de Best joins the firmwide Operating Committee.

Barnum, who has held the role for six years, told the company he intends to conclude his tenure as CFO. The release says he will become a Vice Chairman at that point and has agreed to stay until early 2028. Until the handover he will lead the January and April earnings announcements and the February Investor Day, so the transition is staged rather than abrupt. In the release, chief executive Jamie Dimon said Barnum asked to transition leadership of Finance to another executive.

De Best currently oversees Finance, Business Management and Controls for the Corporate & Investment Bank's Global Banking, Markets, Payments and Securities Services businesses, and was previously co-head of Global Corporate Banking, according to JPMorgan. The company says it will name her successor as the investment bank's CFO early next year. American Banker, which also reported the news, gave her age as 43; the release does not state it, so that figure rests on one outlet.

American Banker framed the announcement against continuing speculation about when Dimon will eventually retire. Neither the company release nor the trade report says anything about a Dimon timetable, so that context is the publication's framing rather than a company statement.

For advisers, a large-bank CFO change matters less for the individual than for what follows it: the investor-day messaging on capital and expenses, the reshuffle of the investment-bank finance team, and the way peers present their own succession plans to shareholders and supervisors.

wire.text: The week in five stories: CrowdStrike's $43.9 billion Zscaler deal, America's Car-Mart's Chapter 11, Nvidia's CEO reversal, Clariant and CD&R's Ashland talks, and EY Canada's $80 million innovation bet.
paras: CrowdStrike agreed to buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valued at about $43.9 billion, with targets of $500 million in cost savings and $1 billion in revenue synergies, the week's largest transaction and a template for security-platform consolidation. America's Car-Mart filed for Chapter 11 with a $10 million stalking-horse bid, a reminder that subprime auto lending stress creates restructuring work.

Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive 11 days after he resigned, putting governance and succession planning in front of every AI-exposed client. Clariant and CD&R confirmed talks to buy Ashland, a possible large chemicals deal that would bring diligence and integration work. EY Canada committed $80 million to AI, quantum and future-of-work bets, a signal of how the large firms are investing in their own capability.

wire.text: Thomson Reuters launches a US$500M share buyback and a new normal course issuer bid for up to 7 million shares.
paras: Thomson Reuters said on 11 November 2026 that it will repurchase up to US$500 million of its shares and has set up a new normal course issuer bid (NCIB), the Canadian mechanism that lets a listed company buy back stock on the open market within set limits.

According to the company's release, the bid covers up to 7 million common shares, about 1.6% of the 433,458,865 shares outstanding at 31 October 2026. It runs from 13 November 2026 to 12 November 2027, and purchases can be made on the TSX, the Nasdaq Global Select Market and other eligible venues. The TSX daily limit is 181,938 shares.

Woodbridge, which holds about 70% of the company, will take part proportionally, with purchases from it starting on 13 November under a TSX exemption. The release says the company bought 6,155,886 shares for US$600 million, an average of US$97.48, under its previous bid. It describes the programme as a flexible way to return capital and says keeping a healthy float is in all shareholders' interest.
For advisers: capital-return policy, float management and the treatment of a controlling holder in a buyback are recurring questions for Canadian listed groups with a dominant shareholder.

bigMoves.title: Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez resigns amid pension-scheme backlog
bigMoves.cs: Government outsourcing recovery, contract-performance reviews, operational turnaround and CEO-transition support; public bodies reassessing large outsourced service contracts.
bigMoves.body: Capita chief executive Adolfo Hernandez stepped down with immediate effect and CFO Pablo Andres replaces him, according to Consultancy.uk.
paras: Capita chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect, and chief financial officer Pablo Andres replaces him, according to Consultancy.uk on 24 November 2026. Hernandez took the job at the start of 2024, succeeding Jon Lewis.

The report links the move to Capita's handling of the Civil Service Pension Scheme, about 1.7 million members, which it took over in December 2025 under a £239 million contract signed by the previous government. The backlog was above 86,000 cases at handover and above 120,000 by early February 2026, and about 8,500 members reportedly had payments delayed. A February government recovery plan added an emergency interest-free loan scheme, 150 civil servants and 100 more Capita staff.

The report says Capita has also warned that its 2027 profit range would be £85 million to £95 million, at least £25 million below earlier expectations. Innovation minister Lilian Greenwood called the problems a 'debacle' days before the resignation, the public accounts committee opened an inquiry earlier this month, and a National Audit Office report is due in the coming months. Ministers have noted the option of returning the contract to government management.

bigMoves.body: LEGO will build a €1 billion factory in Estarreja, Portugal, creating more than 1,000 jobs, with production due in 2030, according to Consultancy.eu.
paras: LEGO has chosen Estarreja, in Portugal's Aveiro district, for a new €1 billion factory expected to create more than 1,000 jobs, according to Consultancy.eu on 25 November 2026. The site covers 60 hectares and could grow to 116; the plant is 115,000 square metres and will handle moulding, processing, packing and warehousing. Construction is expected to start in the first half of 2027, with operations in 2030.

Buck Consultants International advised on location strategy and site selection, a process Consultancy.eu says took about a year. Portuguese newspaper Observador, cited by the report, says Portugal beat at least Spain and Poland. Portugal's trade agency AICEP began talks about a year earlier, and the Estarreja municipality joined in February 2026.

It would be LEGO's fourth European factory and eighth worldwide, after Billund, Kladno and Nyíregyháza in Europe. The report also lists a Vietnam plant opened in April 2025 and a US plant planned for 2027. LEGO targets 100% renewable energy, about 80% of it generated on site, and LEED Platinum certification, according to the report.

For consultants the signal is the mix of work around a plant of this size: site selection and incentive negotiation, supply-chain network design, energy and sustainability engineering, and workforce planning in a region where more than 1,000 hires are needed.
