bigMoves.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns; CFO Colette Kress named interim CEO
bigMoves.cs: CEO-succession and governance advisory, board-effectiveness reviews, investor-communications and risk work for AI-supply-chain customers asking about continuity at their largest chip supplier.
bigMoves.body: Nvidia said on 12 November that Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO and director with immediate effect; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.
paras: Nvidia announced on 12 November 2026 that Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who has held that role since September 2013, is interim CEO and remains CFO. The board is searching for a permanent chief executive and will consider internal and external candidates. Harvey C. Jones, a former chief executive and executive chairman of Synopsys, was appointed the company's first chair of the board.

Nvidia's announcement gives no reason for the resignation. The departure follows a board investigation that the company announced days earlier into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort; the board said then it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Fortune and Al Jazeera, both citing other reporting, say Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and describe reported relationships, including one with a woman U.S. officials reportedly viewed as a Chinese spy. These are reports and allegations. Nvidia has not confirmed them, and whether any intelligence link exists has not been established. Fortune reports that shares fell more than 6% at first on the news. Al Jazeera reports that the market value dipped below $4 trillion, that a shareholder class action has been filed, and that Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress.

Nvidia still reported record third-quarter results on 17 November, covered elsewhere on this site. The unanswered questions are who becomes permanent CEO, how long the interim period lasts, and what the board's investigation finds.
unknowns: Reason for the resignation not given by Nvidia
Outcome of the board's investigation and timing of a permanent CEO not known
Allegations about personal conduct and any intelligence link are reported, not established

bigMoves.title: Sherritt temporarily lays off 280 workers as refining stays halted
bigMoves.cs: Turnaround and liquidity planning, sanctions-licence and supply-chain contingency work, and recapitalisation advisory for a Canadian metals refiner cut off from Cuban feed.
bigMoves.body: Sherritt will temporarily lay off about 280 employees, 47% of its Canadian workforce, for roughly 90 days while its metals refining remains halted.
paras: Sherritt International said on 4 November 2026 that it will temporarily lay off about 280 employees, or 47% of its Canadian workforce, in a release distributed by Business Wire. The layoffs are expected to last about 90 days, and staff may be recalled earlier. Interim chief executive Peter Hancock said the layoffs are intended to be temporary.

The company says refining at its Fort Saskatchewan facility stopped on 22 June 2026 when feed inventory ran out, while ammonia fertiliser and sulphuric acid production continues. Sherritt suspended its direct participation in Cuba joint-venture activity on 7 May 2026, citing U.S. Executive Order 14404, and says it has operated under constrained liquidity conditions. It received its first emergency U.S. Treasury OFAC licence on 19 October 2026.

The release does not say when refining will restart, how remaining regulatory licences will be handled, or where its recapitalisation transaction stands. It also notes that the company's chief human resources officer has left.
unknowns: Recapitalisation status and timing of remaining licences not stated
Restart date for refining not stated

bigMoves.vlabel: Share of global workforce in November round
bigMoves.title: Cisco makes fresh layoffs, cutting under 1% of workforce
bigMoves.cs: Workforce-redesign and operating-model work as large tech firms redeploy spending toward AI; read-across for cost-programme and talent-strategy engagements.
bigMoves.body: Cisco has made another round of job cuts affecting under 1% of its global workforce, according to People Matters, which relies on staff posts and a company statement.
paras: Cisco's latest round of cuts affects less than 1% of its global workforce, according to People Matters on 20 November 2026. The report, based on LinkedIn posts from affected employees, says the cuts happened on 18 November and hit US staff. Cisco did not disclose the teams, locations or number affected, and the article cites a Cisco statement to SDxCentral that winning in the AI era requires focused discipline.

The article puts the longer trend in context: headcount fell by about 8,000, or 8.8%, between July 2024 and July 2026, and Cisco cut about 4,000 jobs in May 2026. It says Cisco expects revenue per employee to rise about 19%, with chief executive Chuck Robbins citing $19 billion in incremental revenue.

People Matters says there is no evidence linking the November cuts to Cisco's work with OpenAI Codex. Because the account rests on employee posts and a statement reported second-hand, the confidence here is Developing.
unknowns: Number of roles, teams and locations affected not disclosed
The Cisco statement is reported second-hand via SDxCentral

bigMoves.vlabel: Anthropic opening pop vs offer price
bigMoves.title: Anthropic opens 34% above offer in first frontier-AI listing
bigMoves.cs: Capital-markets readiness, IPO preparation and valuation work for late-stage AI and tech companies; investor-relations and governance build-outs for new listings.
bigMoves.body: Anthropic's shares opened 34.3% above their offer price on its Nasdaq debut on 19 November, according to a Reuters factbox on 2026 US IPOs.
paras: Anthropic's shares opened 34.3% above their offer price on its Nasdaq debut on Thursday 19 November 2026, according to a Reuters factbox. The factbox calls it the first listing of a frontier AI lab and the second multibillion-dollar IPO this year by a company valued above $1.5 trillion, after SpaceX in June. It does not give Anthropic's offer price.

Reuters lists how other major 2026 US listings opened. Cerebras opened 89% above its $185 offer price in May and raised $5.55 billion. SpaceX opened 11.1% above its $135 offer price in June and raised $75 billion. Bending Spoons opened about 7% above its $29 offer price in July, raising $1.68 billion with selling shareholders. Jersey Mike's opened 8.7% below its $23 offer price in July, raising about $1 billion. vVardis opened 22.2% below its $18 offer price in its November NYSE debut, raising about $175 million.

The spread, from an 89% pop to a 22% drop, shows the window is open but selective. Opening-day moves are not a measure of lasting value, and this factbox does not say how any of the stocks have traded since.
unknowns: Anthropic's offer price is not given in this factbox
Opening-day moves say little about later trading

bigMoves.title: Intuit agrees to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
bigMoves.cs: Separation and transition-services work for the carved-out unit, integration and cost-take-out planning for the buyer, and capital-allocation advice for Intuit as it recycles cash into buybacks.
bigMoves.body: Intuit has agreed to sell its Mailchimp marketing platform to Italy's Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, with closing expected in early 2027.
paras: Intuit said on 19 November 2026, alongside its first-quarter results, that it has agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68 billion, made up of $3.31 billion in cash and $368 million in Bending Spoons stock. Bending Spoons' own release describes an all-cash enterprise value of $3.68 billion in which Intuit reinvests $368 million into newly issued Bending Spoons equity. The two companies describe the same figures in different words, so the structure should be read from the filings. Closing is expected in early calendar year 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary conditions.

Intuit's release shows why the unit may have become a candidate for sale. Mailchimp revenue fell 1% to $313 million in the quarter ended 31 October 2026, while Intuit's total revenue rose 12% to $4.4 billion. Intuit said it plans to use the cash proceeds to repurchase shares in fiscal 2027 after the deal closes, and its guidance excludes the sale until then. Bending Spoons buys 100% of The Rocket Science Group, LLC and other Mailchimp assets and liabilities; its board approved the deal unanimously. Citi and J.P. Morgan advised Bending Spoons, with Freshfields as legal counsel and EY-Parthenon on financial due diligence.

Bending Spoons chief executive Luca Ferrari said the company will invest substantially in the business after closing. Neither release gives plans for pricing, products or customer data, which is what Mailchimp's customers and partners will watch.
unknowns: Post-closing plans for pricing, product and data were not disclosed
Exact closing date and purchase price allocation were not disclosed

bigMoves.title: Plus Ultra seeks creditor protection, cuts most routes and 679 jobs
bigMoves.cs: Airline restructuring and turnaround work, fleet and ACMI wet-lease strategy, and labour-negotiation support; read-across for carriers exposed to fuel costs.
bigMoves.body: Spanish carrier Plus Ultra has told a Madrid court it has begun creditor talks, and has issued a redundancy notice covering 679 employees.
paras: Plus Ultra Líneas Aéreas filed a pre-insolvency notice with Madrid Commercial Court No. 8 on 13 November 2026, according to Aviacionline, giving it three months, extendable by three, to agree a restructuring plan with creditors. The airline served a collective redundancy notice on 12 November covering 679 employees, the outlet reports, citing the UGT union, and also plans a temporary layoff procedure and a smaller fleet of Airbus A330s.

AeroTime reports that scheduled flying would shrink to Caracas–Madrid and Tenerife North, with most activity shifting to ACMI wet-leasing, and that the airline blames fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict. Aviacionline gives operating losses of €31.08 million between February and August and projected 2026 fuel spending of €104.83 million against a €69.13 million budget. AeroTime describes the loss figure as unverified Spanish media reporting.

Aviacionline adds that the airline asked Spain's state holding company SEPI to defer by two years repayment of the first €19 million of a €53 million 2021 rescue package, and that the chairman and chief executive lost their powers in July and later stepped down. AeroTime says Volotea also filed for creditor protection in September 2026. Both outlets rely partly on unnamed or unverified sources, so the figures are best read as reported.
unknowns: Final restructuring plan and number of redundancies not known
Whether the Lima and Buenos Aires route halts become permanent is unclear

bigMoves.vlabel: Pledged by BC Partners Credit; deal failed
bigMoves.title: LIV Golf files Chapter 11 plan for orderly wind-down
bigMoves.cs: Wind-down and liquidation-trust advisory, creditor and contract unwinding, and sports-media rights repricing as a major league funder exits.
bigMoves.body: LIV Golf has filed a Chapter 11 plan in New Jersey for an orderly wind-down after its main backer stopped funding it, according to the Associated Press.
paras: LIV Golf filed a Chapter 11 plan in New Jersey on 10 November 2026 setting out an orderly wind-down, according to the Associated Press. The league entered bankruptcy on 8 September after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund stopped funding it following the 2026 season. A restructuring deal with BC Partners Credit, which had pledged $300 million, did not win enough support to create a new version of the league, the AP reports.

The filing says the Public Investment Fund put in about $5 billion of equity, the AP reports. It also says 289 employees were laid off and 22 furloughed about a week before the filing, and that $15.6 million in retention bonuses went to seven executives. LIV's own summary says no viable restructuring transaction remains, according to the report.

The plan would route proceeds to creditors through a wind-down trust. The AP's account of court hearing dates is unclear, so the schedule should be checked against the court docket. Creditor claim totals and the final liquidation timeline are not stated in the article.
unknowns: Creditor claim totals and liquidation timing not stated
Court hearing dates need checking against the docket

bigMoves.title: Children's Place files Chapter 11 and seeks to sell its assets
bigMoves.cs: Retail restructuring and liquidation advisory, lease and store-portfolio decisions, and carve-out and bid support for buyers of a kids' apparel brand.
bigMoves.body: The Children's Place has filed Chapter 11 in New Jersey and plans to sell substantially all of its assets by the end of December 2026.
paras: The Children's Place filed Chapter 11 petitions in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey, according to a company release cited by Bloomberg Law on 9 November 2026. The retailer says it intends to sell substantially all of its assets and expects the sale process to finish by the end of December 2026. Bids are due on 9 December.

The company says it is talking with multiple parties about transactions that would let the business keep operating, and plans a new term loan from its existing secured lenders. Its stores and e-commerce sites remain open during the process, according to the report.

The readable part of the article does not give debt totals, store counts or the reasons for the filing, so those details are unknown here. For consultants, a sale on this timetable means fast work on store-by-store economics, lease negotiations, inventory valuation and transition planning for whoever buys the brand.
unknowns: Debt totals, store counts and stated reasons for the filing were not available
Identity of bidders not disclosed

bigMoves.vlabel: Sale price; about $1.1B net cash expected
bigMoves.title: Textron sells industrial segment to Kingswood Capital for $1.2 billion
bigMoves.cs: Carve-out, separation and TSA work for Kautex and the Specialized Vehicles brands; buyer-side integration and value-creation plans; capital-allocation advice as Textron refocuses on aerospace and defence.
bigMoves.body: Textron has agreed to sell its Industrial segment, including Kautex and its Specialized Vehicles brands, to an affiliate of Kingswood Capital Management for $1.2 billion, according to trade reports.
paras: Textron agreed on 18 November 2026 to sell its Industrial segment to an affiliate of Los Angeles-based Kingswood Capital Management for $1.2 billion, according to Air Data News, PlasticsToday and Finchannel, which all report the same terms. Textron expects about $1.1 billion of net cash after taxes and transaction costs, and closing is expected in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.

The segment includes Kautex and Textron Specialized Vehicles, whose brands include E-Z-GO, Cushman, Jacobsen and Ransomes, the outlets report. Textron will keep Textron Aviation, Bell and Textron Systems and, according to Air Data News, put the Industrial segment into discontinued operations from the fourth quarter of 2026. It expects a non-cash pre-tax impairment of $350 million to $400 million in that quarter, the report says, citing its SEC filing. The board also authorised repurchases of up to 35 million shares, per the reports, and Goldman Sachs and Latham & Watkins advised Textron, according to PlasticsToday.

FlightGlobal's earlier headline described the move as a spin-off; the trade reports describe a sale to private equity. Kingswood manages about $7.1 billion in assets, per PlasticsToday. Textron's own release and SEC filing were not readable in this run, so the figures above are as reported by the outlets.
unknowns: Buyer financing terms and the fate of Industrial employees were not reported
Textron's release and SEC filing were not read; figures are as reported by trade outlets

bigMoves.vlabel: Partnership for up to 1GW of UK data-centre capacity
bigMoves.title: Drax, Brookfield and Radiant plan £20bn, 1GW UK data centre
bigMoves.cs: Site, grid-connection and power-sourcing strategy, planning and regulatory approvals, and tenant-sourcing work for AI data-centre developments on power-station sites.
bigMoves.body: Drax, Brookfield and Radiant have agreed a £20 billion partnership to deliver up to 1GW of UK data-centre capacity at Drax Power Station.
paras: Drax, Brookfield and Brookfield's neocloud platform Radiant have agreed a £20 billion partnership (about US$26.8 billion) to deliver up to 1GW of UK data-centre capacity, according to Construction Briefing on 3 November 2026. The site is Drax Power Station near Selby in North Yorkshire.

The first 100MW phase could receive up to £2.5 billion of backing from the Brookfield-Qai AI infrastructure joint venture, the article says, and could be running from the first quarter of 2028. Capacity could then ramp to 500MW between 2028 and 2031. Phase one depends on planning, regulatory and grid approvals and on finding a tenant.

Drax chief executive Will Gardiner said the company is proud to partner with leading AI infrastructure providers on the project. The tenant and final investment decision are not yet known, which is where most of the delivery risk sits.
unknowns: Tenant and final investment decision not announced
Planning, regulatory and grid approvals still required

bigMoves.title: Deloitte wins Valterra Platinum finance, HR and payroll outsourcing
bigMoves.cs: Outsourcing and transition work for miners separating from a parent; shows Big Four firms pushing operate services beyond advice, with Deloitte targeting 30%+ of revenue from outsourcing.
bigMoves.body: Valterra Platinum, formerly Anglo American Platinum, has signed an outsourcing agreement under which Deloitte South Africa runs its finance, HR and payroll functions; 130+ staff transfer, according to Consultancy.co.za.
paras: Valterra Platinum, the Johannesburg-based miner formerly known as Anglo American Platinum, has signed a business process outsourcing agreement with Deloitte, according to Consultancy.co.za on 20 November 2026. Deloitte will take over corporate support functions including finance, HR and payroll through its Finance and HR Operate practice.

More than 130 Valterra employees are moving to Deloitte's South African operations, the article says, and the appointment followed a competitive process. Valterra became an independent company in 2025.

Ruwayda Redfearn, chief executive of Deloitte's Africa business unit, is quoted saying the deal advances its ambition to scale outsourcing; the article cites a goal of more than 30% of revenue from outsource services. Valterra chief executive Craig Miller calls it an important step.
unknowns: Contract value and term not disclosed

bigMoves.title: Teneo hires Roland Berger nuclear lead for energy practice
bigMoves.cs: Shows demand for nuclear and power-sector advice and the talent race for it; utilities and developers get another adviser with nuclear depth.
bigMoves.body: Teneo has hired Mike Granowski, a seven-year Roland Berger partner and its global nuclear technology lead, as senior managing director in energy and infrastructure, based in Chicago, according to Consulting.us.
paras: Teneo has hired Mike Granowski as a senior managing director in its energy and infrastructure practice, according to Consulting.us on 20 November 2026. He will be based in Chicago and support clients in nuclear energy and the broader power and gas sector.

Granowski has more than 25 years of consulting experience. He comes from Roland Berger, where he spent seven years as a partner, global nuclear technology lead and North American energy and utilities platform lead. Earlier roles included Enovation Partners, Bridge Strategy Group and Navigant, and he began as a nuclear engineer at Commonwealth Edison.
Dan Gabaldon, Teneo's vice chairman for management consulting and head of energy, welcomed the hire. Consulting.us puts Teneo at more than 1,800 people in over 50 offices.
unknowns: Whether a team follows

bigMoves.title: Oliver Wyman to acquire Synpulse in its largest deal
bigMoves.cs: Integration, brand and talent-retention work for the combined firm; for banks and insurers, a new option for strategy-to-build programmes and a vendor-landscape check on who now owns delivery.
bigMoves.body: Oliver Wyman has agreed to acquire Synpulse, a financial services consultancy of about 1,200 people, which Consultancy.eu calls its largest acquisition. Terms are undisclosed; closing is expected in early 2027.
paras: Oliver Wyman, the management consultancy in the Marsh McLennan group, has agreed to acquire Synpulse, a financial services consultancy with about 1,200 professionals across Europe, Asia and North America, according to Consultancy.eu on 19 November 2026. The publication describes it as the largest acquisition in Oliver Wyman's history. No price or deal terms were disclosed, and the transaction is expected to close in early 2027.

Synpulse was founded in 1996 and sells consulting and technology services: enterprise systems modernisation, digital product development and AI solution implementation. It also runs a technology division, Synpulse8, which works with more than 100 technology partners. The firm is co-headquartered in Switzerland and Singapore, with about 550 staff in each, and has roughly 100 people in the United States and Canada, per Consultancy.eu.

The deal is Oliver Wyman's second acquisition this year, after the US restructuring firm CR3 Partners. Consultancy.eu puts Oliver Wyman at more than 7,000 staff in over 70 offices, which would pass 8,000 people once Synpulse is included. Synpulse is to keep its brand and leadership team, and the article gives no long-term integration plan. Ted Moynihan, Oliver Wyman's chief executive, and Konrad Niggli and Yves Roesti, Synpulse's co-chief executives, are quoted in the announcement coverage.
unknowns: Deal terms were not disclosed

bigMoves.title: Bishop Fleming buys Kilsby Williams, entering South Wales
bigMoves.cs: Integration, back-office and client-migration work for a PE-backed accountancy consolidator; mid-market owners weighing a sale get a read on how backed firms buy regional practices.
bigMoves.body: UK accountancy and advisory firm Bishop Fleming has acquired Kilsby Williams, a South Wales firm of about 80 people, giving it a tenth office. Terms were not disclosed.
paras: Bishop Fleming, a UK audit, accountancy, tax and advisory firm, has acquired Kilsby Williams, an independent accounting and advisory practice in South Wales, according to Consultancy.uk on 20 November 2026. The deal adds around 80 staff and gives Bishop Fleming its first presence in the region, taking it to ten offices across the West Midlands, South West and Wales.

Kilsby Williams was founded in 1991 and reported revenue of about £7.5 million in its latest financial year. It will keep operating from its Newport office, initially under its own name, while integration continues. Bishop Fleming says the combined firm has well over 600 people and approaches 70 partners.

The article describes this as Bishop Fleming's first acquisition since a minority investment from private equity investor Synova in 2025. Andrew Sandiford, Bishop Fleming's chief executive and managing partner, called it an important moment for the firm. Simon Tee, Kilsby Williams' managing partner, said the firm can keep what clients value while gaining scale and investment. Price, closing date and any integration timetable were not stated.

Integration timetable

bigMoves.vlabel: Mercator, US ports and maritime adviser
bigMoves.title: Steer acquires US maritime consultancy Mercator
bigMoves.cs: Port, terminal and shipping strategy, commercial due diligence and transaction advisory; a larger maritime bench for infrastructure investors.
bigMoves.body: UK-based Steer has acquired Mercator, a Kirkland, Washington consultancy advising ports, terminals and shipping on strategy, commercial and transaction work, according to Consultancy.uk. Price was not stated.
paras: Steer, the UK-headquartered transport and infrastructure consultancy, has acquired Mercator, a US maritime and ports adviser, Consultancy.uk reported on 18 November 2026. The deal strengthens Steer's work in ports, maritime transport and freight advisory.

Mercator has been based in Kirkland, Washington, since 2000. It advises investors, port authorities, terminal operators, shipping companies and logistics businesses on strategy, commercial matters and transactions. The article says it has completed more than 150 commercial due diligence projects and advised over 40 investors and financial institutions. Named projects include advice to the Ports of Seattle and Tacoma on forming the Northwest Seaport Alliance, to the Quebec Port Authority on a new container terminal, and to a Macquarie-led consortium on its acquisition of Long Beach Container Terminal.

Steer was founded in 1978 and has 29 offices across Europe, North America, Latin America and Asia. This is its fourth acquisition since 2021, following Fourth Economy in the US and Amberside Advisors and Evolution Infrastructure in the UK. Mercator will join Steer's North American division, keep its brand and keep its leadership. Steer chief executive Hugh Jones said the deal will strengthen the firm's offer beyond North America.
unknowns: Deal terms were not disclosed

bigMoves.title: Finyx acquires Birmingham consultancy Entec Si
bigMoves.cs: Public-sector and not-for-profit advisory capacity is being consolidated by mid-sized technology consultancies, creating integration and local-government transformation work.
bigMoves.body: Finyx Group, a London-based technology and transformation consultancy with more than 100 consultants, has acquired Entec Si, a Birmingham firm of about 20 core staff, according to Consultancy.uk.
paras: Finyx Group, a technology and transformation consultancy with offices in London, Belfast and York and more than 100 consultants, has acquired Entec Si, a Birmingham consultancy founded in 1996 by Peter Marsden, Consultancy.uk reported on 18 November 2026.

Entec Si has about 20 core staff plus associates and focuses on local government and not-for-profit clients, with work in healthcare, transport, aviation and higher education. No price or terms were given.

The deal follows Finyx's April 2026 purchase of Woodhurst, a 30-person financial services consultancy. Entec Si managing director Eman Al-Hillawi and Finyx chief executive Phil Stewart are quoted in the report.
unknowns: Deal terms were not disclosed

bigMoves.title: KFC franchisee Tasty Chick'n files Chapter 11 with 84 restaurants
bigMoves.cs: Turnaround, franchise-system and real-estate advisory: franchisee distress, remodel mandates and royalty disputes are a pattern franchisors and lenders must plan for.
bigMoves.body: Tasty Chick'n, a KFC and Taco Bell franchisee, filed for Chapter 11 on 16 November in Texas, citing falling sales, thin margins and franchisor demands, and plans a court-supervised sale.
paras: Tasty Chick'n LLC and three affiliates filed for Chapter 11 protection on 16 November 2026 in the US Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas, according to National Restaurant News and TheStreet (via Yahoo). The operator runs 84 restaurants in ten states: 75 KFC units and nine KFC/Taco Bell co-branded units.

The filings put numbers on the squeeze. NRN reports nearly $73 million of funded debt. TheStreet, citing court papers, reports assets of $50 million to $100 million and liabilities of $100 million to $500 million. The company's papers say sales fell 11.4% in fiscal 2024, 1.4% in 2025 and 2.8% so far in 2026, while restaurant-level margin dropped from 11.8% in fiscal 2023 to 4% this year. Trailing restaurant EBITDA was about $7.1 million against $12.4 million a year earlier, per TheStreet.

The papers also describe a dispute with the franchisor. Royalty deferrals began in mid-2025, a notice of breach followed in December 2025, and a notice of intent to terminate was issued on 15 September 2026, with unpaid royalties and fees cited at roughly $15.6 million to $15.7 million. The company also points to franchisor-required remodels at nearly 40 restaurants through 2029 as a cost it says it cannot carry.

To fund the case, the company has arranged a debtor-in-possession facility of up to $20 million from its prepetition lender, MidCap Financial Trust: $5 million of new money and a $15 million roll-up. No reorganisation plan has been described; the stated aim is a court-supervised sale, either as one portfolio or market by market. These are the company's claims in court filings, and the franchisor's position has not been reported in the sources we read.

For advisers, the case is a template: a mid-size franchisee squeezed between falling traffic, rising costs and brand-mandated capital spending. It points to work for lenders and landlords valuing a sale by market, for franchisors deciding how hard to enforce remodel schedules, and for other multi-unit operators stress-testing their own covenants.
unknowns: Whether Yum Brands or the franchisor will comment or support the sale
Bid timeline and the buyer pool
Final creditor list and recoveries
questions: A multi-unit franchisee misses royalty payments while a brand demands remodels; how do you advise its lender?

bigMoves.vlabel: McKinsey and Cognition (Devin) to sell AI software engineering
bigMoves.title: McKinsey and Cognition ally to sell AI software engineering
bigMoves.cs: Direct read-across for consulting: McKinsey is packaging implementation of AI coding agents, with baselines for cost, speed and quality, as a service line; rivals and clients' engineering leaders must decide who owns that work.
bigMoves.body: McKinsey and Cognition, maker of the Devin AI software engineer, announced an alliance on 16 November to help large companies capture value from AI-driven software engineering.
paras: McKinsey & Company and Cognition, the maker of the Devin autonomous software engineer, announced an alliance on 16 November 2026, according to McKinsey's alliances blog. McKinsey says it will help clients prioritise high-value engineering work, set baselines for cost, speed and quality, and scale new ways of working, while Cognition supplies Devin, which it describes as model-agnostic.

McKinsey cites its own second-quarter 2026 survey of 334 product and engineering leaders: the top 25% reported productivity gains of more than 2x, while nearly 30% reported declining productivity. The firm also says it has helped more than 50 companies rewire for AI-powered software development. The Next Web, which reported the news the same day, says the two will sell the offering to large companies in the US and Europe. Cognition's claims of lower cost through model routing and of clients among large banks and insurers are the company's own and were not independently verified.

A McKinsey senior partner, Saptarshi Ganguly, is quoted saying doubling productivity takes more than deploying agents. The page does not state financial terms, an effective date beyond publication, or whether the alliance is exclusive.

The read-across for the industry is that a leading strategy firm is tying its change-management and baselining work to a specific agent vendor. That is a template other firms are likely to copy with other vendors, and a reason for engineering leaders to ask what independent measurement they get.
unknowns: Financial terms and exclusivity
Independent verification of the survey and case results
Whether other firms announce comparable alliances

bigMoves.title: Merck KGaA agrees to buy Rapid Micro Biosystems at $0.75 a share
bigMoves.cs: Deal-readiness, integration and carve-in work for life-science tools buyers; distressed small-cap targets are being absorbed by strategics.
bigMoves.body: Merck KGaA signed a definitive agreement on 16 November to buy Rapid Micro Biosystems through a cash tender offer at $0.75 a share, with closing expected in December.
paras: Rapid Micro Biosystems said on 16 November 2026 that it signed a definitive agreement to be acquired by Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany. Under the agreement, a Merck KGaA subsidiary, EMD Holdings NewCo II, Inc., will launch a tender offer for all shares at $0.75 in cash, followed by a merger.

The company's release says closing is expected in December 2026, subject to a minimum tender condition and customary conditions; it does not specify regulatory approvals. Perella Weinberg Partners is the company's financial adviser and Goodwin Procter LLP its legal counsel. InsideArbitrage, an event-driven deal newsletter, puts the premium at 15.38% and the deal value at about $39 million; the release itself does not state either figure, so we treat them as the newsletter's calculation.

The deal is small by value but it is a clear pattern: a strategic buyer in life-science tools picking up a quality-control automation business at a low absolute price. For consultants, the work is in integration of manufacturing-quality products into a larger life-science portfolio, customer-overlap analysis and the buyer's own technology roadmap. What the release does not say is why Merck KGaA wants the business or what it plans for the product line, so those are unknowns.
unknowns: Merck KGaA's strategic rationale and integration plans
Regulatory approvals required
Final tender acceptance level
questions: A strategic buyer acquires a small automation-tools business at a low price; how do you size the integration opportunity?

bigMoves.title: Rosemont Pharmaceuticals agrees to buy Aytu BioPharma at $2.70 a share
bigMoves.cs: Specialty-pharma integration, portfolio-fit and commercial-model work for acquirers of small branded-drug companies.
bigMoves.body: Rosemont Pharmaceuticals Holdings agreed on 16 November to buy Aytu BioPharma for $2.70 a share in cash via a tender offer, with closing expected by the end of 2026.
paras: Aytu BioPharma announced on 16 November 2026 that it will be acquired by Rosemont Pharmaceuticals Holdings, based in Leeds in the UK, for $2.70 per share in cash. The deal is structured as a tender offer, to be launched within ten business days, followed by a second-step merger at the same price, according to an exhibit filed with the SEC.

The company's release says the price is a 41.1% premium to the 30-day volume-weighted average price and 51.7% to the 13 November close. InsideArbitrage reports a premium of 48.35%, so the basis differs between sources; we use the company's figures. Aytu's board approved unanimously, and holders including Nantahala Capital Management and Stonepine Capital Management, plus Aytu's officers and directors, signed support agreements. Conditions include a majority tender and the exercise or termination of certain warrants, and closing is expected in late December.

Canaccord Genuity and Dorsey & Whitney advised Aytu; Bourne Partners and Ropes & Gray advised Rosemont. For advisers, the transaction shows a private specialty-pharma buyer taking a listed small cap private, which typically creates work in commercial integration, supply-chain rationalisation and financing. The release does not describe Rosemont's plans for Aytu's products, so we cannot say more.
unknowns: Rosemont's plans for the product portfolio
Financing details
Final tender acceptance
questions: How do you test portfolio fit when a private pharma company acquires a listed specialty-drug business?

bigMoves.title: Nvidia's board opens a probe into CEO Jensen Huang
bigMoves.body: Independent directors launched an investigation into reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The board says it has no reason to believe company information was compromised, and the allegations have not been established.
bigMoves.cs: A live case of key-person risk at a $4.5 trillion company. Boards and their advisers will be stress-testing succession plans.
bigMoves.take: Whatever the probe finds, every board just got a reminder to have a real succession plan.

bigMoves.vlabel: roadshow range; priced Nov 18 at $83 (see lead story)
bigMoves.title: Anthropic roadshow launches at $70–78; IPO later priced at $83
bigMoves.cs: Mega-IPOs mean months of readiness work: governance, controls and investor storytelling.
bigMoves.body: Anthropic launched its roadshow on 10 November for about 825 million Class A shares. On 18 November AP reported pricing at $83 a share, above the range, for 980 million shares.
paras: Anthropic announced on 10 November that it has launched the roadshow for its initial public offering. The company says it is offering 825,000,000 Class A shares, about 801 million from the company and about 24 million from selling stockholders, with underwriters holding a 30-day option on up to 123.75 million more. The expected range is $70 to $78 a share, for a Nasdaq Global Select listing under the ticker ANT. The registration statement has been filed but is not yet effective.

RTTNews reports a concurrent $26 billion private placement of Class N stock at the IPO price to partners including AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC. Bloomberg, as relayed by StockAnalysis, says the book is several times oversubscribed and reports implied valuations of roughly $1.0 trillion on shares outstanding and $1.4 trillion fully diluted. These oversubscription and valuation figures are press-reported, not company statements.

Update, 18 November: AP reports the IPO priced at $83 a share, above the range, for 980 million shares and about $81 billion, valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion. See the separate pricing story.
Disclosure: The Consultant Times' automated editor is built on Anthropic's Claude.
unknowns: First-day trading, which comes after Nov 18

bigMoves.title: Marvell's Lumentum deal dwarfs every other AI acquisition this month
bigMoves.cs: Chip supply chains are consolidating. Integration at this scale is huge advisory work.

bigMoves.title: Ottawa agrees to invest up to $1.14B in Cohere
bigMoves.cs: Sovereign AI is now industrial policy. Expect public-sector AI strategy work in Canada.

bigMoves.title: Shield AI buys Echodyne for $5.3B and more than doubles its valuation
bigMoves.cs: Defence tech is consolidating fast, a growing niche for strategy and deal teams.

bigMoves.title: Salesforce agrees to buy AI customer-service firm Cresta
bigMoves.cs: Software giants are buying AI features rather than building them, then need integration help.

bigMoves.title: BMO and RBC sell Moneris to Francisco Partners
bigMoves.body: The two banks, which each held 50%, agreed to sell their payments processor in an all-cash deal. They keep exclusive customer-referral arrangements. RBC expects an after-tax gain of about C$475 million and BMO about C$600 million.
bigMoves.cs: Banks are separating ownership of payment infrastructure from the distribution of it. Expect more carve-outs and referral-model deals.
bigMoves.take: The banks keep the customer and hand off the capital-heavy part.

bigMoves.title: Revolut closes a secondary share sale at a $115 billion valuation
bigMoves.body: The round values the UK neobank at $115 billion, up from $75 billion a year ago, making it Europe's most valuable private company. It reported pre-tax profit of £1.7 billion for 2025 on revenue of £4.5 billion.
bigMoves.cs: Digital banks now trade as global platforms. Incumbent banks benchmark cost-to-serve and product breadth against them.
bigMoves.take: Profit, not just growth, is what supports the price.

bigMoves.title: OpenAI banks about $11 billion of a round valued at $1.25 trillion
bigMoves.body: Bloomberg reported that the first portion has been wired, with the round possibly reaching $20 billion. OpenAI first sought $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, and its March round raised $122 billion at $852 billion. OpenAI declined to comment.
bigMoves.cs: A smaller, lower-valued round than planned suggests investors are more selective about AI infrastructure spending.
bigMoves.take: Still the biggest private valuation ever, but below the original ask.

bigMoves.title: Cerebras prices its IPO at $185, raising $5.55 billion
bigMoves.body: The AI chipmaker sold 30 million shares above its marketed range, in the largest US IPO of 2026 at the time. Reuters reports a fully diluted valuation of about $56 billion; demand ran at more than 20 times the shares offered. A $20 billion OpenAI compute deal underpins the story.
bigMoves.cs: The IPO shows public investors will fund AI hardware that challenges Nvidia, though customer concentration remains a risk.
bigMoves.take: Customer concentration with OpenAI is the thing to watch.

bigMoves.title: Fox shareholders and Roku holders approve the $160-a-share takeover
bigMoves.body: Fox is paying $96 in cash and 0.9693 Fox Class A shares per Roku share. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 but faces a second DOJ request for information. Fox expects about $400 million of run-rate cost savings.
bigMoves.cs: A broadcaster buying a streaming platform. Expect work on integration, ad-tech and distribution-terms negotiations.
bigMoves.take: Antitrust review, not shareholders, is the real gate.

bigMoves.title: BCE sells almost half of a new wireless-tower company to La Caisse
bigMoves.body: The new TowerCo holds more than 5,000 Bell tower sites. BCE keeps control and says the sale supports its goal of cutting net debt leverage to 3.5 times by the end of 2027.
bigMoves.cs: A pension fund buys stable infrastructure cash flow while the telco funds AI data centres and fibre. A template for other carriers.
bigMoves.take: BCE keeps control but monetizes the asset.

bigMoves.title: Accenture spent $4.9 billion on 17 acquisitions in fiscal 2026 and plans about $5 billion more
bigMoves.body: The deal pace supports its fiscal 2027 growth guide, which includes 2 to 2.5 points from acquisitions. Accenture raised $5 billion of debt in the fourth quarter.
bigMoves.cs: A leading consulting firm is buying AI, data and safety capabilities rather than building them. Boutiques are acquisition targets.

bigMoves.title: OpenAI launches a $4 billion deployment company and Bain, McKinsey and Capgemini join as partners
bigMoves.body: The new business is majority-owned by OpenAI, led by TPG with Advent, Bain Capital and Brookfield, and began by acquiring the 150-person consulting firm Tomoro. Bain's investment focuses on private equity clients and their portfolio companies.
bigMoves.cs: An AI lab is building its own consulting arm while consulting firms invest in it. Consultants should expect more partnership and competition at the same time.
bigMoves.take: Model makers are moving into the services layer, which makes the firms partners and rivals.

bigMoves.vlabel: Cut to midpoint of 2026 revenue guidance
bigMoves.title: Gildan slashes 2026 outlook and withdraws its 2028 targets after a weak third quarter
bigMoves.cs: Integration re-plan and cost programmes for the HanesBrands combination, working-capital and inventory reviews with distributors, and wholesale demand forecasting work across apparel supply chains.
bigMoves.body: Gildan cut its 2026 revenue guidance to $5.4-5.5 billion from $6.0-6.2 billion and withdrew its 2026-2028 targets, according to FashionUnited.
paras: Gildan Activewear reported third-quarter results on 5 November 2026 and lowered its full-year outlook sharply, according to FashionUnited. Revenue guidance now stands at $5.4-5.5 billion, down from $6.0-6.2 billion, adjusted EPS at $3.70-3.80 from $4.65-4.75, and adjusted operating margin at about 20% from about 21.8%. The company also withdrew its three-year 2026-2028 targets, the outlet reports. CTV News reported that the shares fell about 25 per cent on the day.

Quarterly net sales from continuing operations were $1.47 billion, up 61.1% because of the HanesBrands integration, per FashionUnited, but wholesale revenue fell 6.8%. Management pointed to softer consumer demand, distributors cutting replenishment orders to manage working capital, and cautious inventory commitments from retail partners. Adjusted margin was helped by $177 million of tariff refunds, the report says. Gildan also sold HanesBrands Australia for about A$700 million and left net leverage at 2.7 times.
unknowns: Whether the demand weakness is temporary destocking or a lasting shift was not stated
Gildan's own release was not read; figures come from FashionUnited and CTV News

bigMoves.title: Walmart raises its full-year outlook as e-commerce and advertising keep outgrowing stores
bigMoves.cs: Omnichannel and retail-media strategy work for competitors, membership-model and pricing reviews, and supply-chain and fulfilment-cost programmes as the market leader widens its lead.
bigMoves.body: Walmart reported third-quarter revenue of $188.8 billion, up 5.2%, and raised its full-year sales and profit outlook, according to Supermarket News.
paras: Walmart reported third-quarter revenue of $188.8 billion on 19 November 2026, up 5.2%, with adjusted EPS of $0.65, according to Supermarket News and StockAnalysis. Walmart U.S. e-commerce grew 23%, Sam's Club U.S. e-commerce 30%, and global advertising 25%, the first outlet reports. Global membership fee revenue rose 17%.

The company raised its fiscal 2027 outlook to net sales growth of 4.9-5.2%, adjusted operating income growth of 8-8.6% and adjusted EPS of $2.84-2.89 in constant currency, per the same reports. StockAnalysis says the sales outlook remains below analyst expectations and notes Walmart U.S. comparable sales of 2.9%. The reports flag a roughly 70 basis point headwind in health and wellness from deflation tied to drug price regulation, and pressure on Sam's Club operating income from a new bundled membership and a LIFO charge.
unknowns: Walmart's own release was not read; the two outlets differ on the prior guidance ranges, so none are quoted here
Share-price reaction was not confirmed

bigMoves.vlabel: Per-share tariff refund inside Q3 EPS
bigMoves.title: Lowe's beats on EPS, but a $250 million tariff refund flatters the quarter
bigMoves.cs: Margin-bridge and gross-margin diagnostics after acquisitions, tariff-refund accounting and pricing reviews, and Pro-customer strategy work as DIY demand stays soft.
bigMoves.body: Lowe's reported third-quarter sales of $22.8 billion, up 9.3%, with about $250 million of IEEPA tariff refunds adding $0.34 to EPS, according to its release.
paras: Lowe's reported third-quarter sales of $22.8 billion on 18 November 2026, up 9.3%, with comparable sales up 1.8%, its sixth straight positive quarter, according to its earnings release filed with the SEC. Adjusted EPS was $3.10 and online sales rose 17.4%. Gross margin fell to 32.95% from 34.19%.

The release says IEEPA tariff refunds added about $250 million before tax, or $0.34 per share. Zacks, via Finviz, calculates that excluding the refund adjusted EPS would have been about $2.76, below consensus. Full-year guidance is for sales of about $92.5 billion, comparable sales up about 0.5% and adjusted EPS of about $12.25; Zacks says the EPS figure is unchanged from August, which implies a lower underlying outlook. Shares were down about 4% premarket, per the same report. Acquisitions of Foundation Building Materials and Artisan Design Group added about 7.5 points of sales growth, according to Zacks.
unknowns: The release does not say whether refunds are included in full-year guidance
The underlying-earnings calculation is Zacks' analysis, not the company's

bigMoves.title: Cisco posts record $18.5 billion quarter and raises FY27 guidance on AI networking demand
bigMoves.cs: AI data-centre and network-modernisation programmes for enterprises and telcos, supply-chain sourcing work around optics, and vendor-selection support as networking spend recovers.
bigMoves.body: Cisco reported record first-quarter revenue of $18.5 billion, up 24%, and raised its fiscal 2027 outlook, according to Fierce Network.
paras: Cisco reported first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $18.5 billion, up 24% year on year, with networking product orders up 28%, according to Fierce Network and Constellation Research. Non-GAAP EPS was $1.40, seven cents above Wall Street estimates, per Constellation.

Cisco guided fiscal 2027 revenue to $74.8-75.8 billion and non-GAAP EPS to $5.47-5.53, against consensus of about $73.2 billion and $5.15, according to Constellation. Fierce Network reports that hyperscaler AI infrastructure revenue is expected to reach about $9 billion in fiscal 2027, more than double fiscal 2026. Orders excluding hyperscalers rose 14%, the outlet says, and CEO Chuck Robbins described a multi-year networking supercycle. CFO Mark Patterson said optics is the tightest part of the supply chain, per the same report.
unknowns: How much of the growth reaches enterprise buyers rather than hyperscalers and service providers
Share-price reaction was not confirmed

bigMoves.vlabel: Premarket share move after first 2026 guidance cut
bigMoves.title: YETI trims its 2026 outlook as U.S. direct-to-consumer demand softens
bigMoves.cs: Channel-mix and direct-to-consumer reviews, international expansion planning, and pricing and promotion strategy as a premium brand loses online momentum.
bigMoves.body: YETI reported third-quarter sales of $509.4 million, up 4%, and cut its 2026 adjusted sales growth outlook to about 6% from 7-8%, according to its release.
paras: YETI reported third-quarter sales of $509.4 million on 12 November 2026, up 4%, with wholesale up 19% but direct-to-consumer down 6%, according to its earnings release. Adjusted EPS rose 49% to $0.91 on adjusted gross margin of 59%.

The company cut 2026 adjusted sales growth to about 6% from 7-8%, and adjusted EPS to $2.90-2.95 from $2.94-3.00, per the release. Stocktwits reports the shares fell about 11% premarket and quotes CEO Matt Reintjes citing uneven demand in the U.S. and Canada, weak online and Amazon channels, and a cautious consumer who could weigh on the fourth quarter. International sales rose 19% and U.S. sales 1%, the release shows. YETI also changed how it reports adjusted results, excluding recall reserve adjustments and a tariff refund benefit, so comparisons with earlier periods are not like for like.
unknowns: Where the closing share price settled was not confirmed
Fourth-quarter trend after the holiday season is unknown

bigMoves.title: Treasury fines Bank of America more than $1.2 billion over money-laundering and sanctions failures
bigMoves.cs: AML lookbacks and independent reviews, transaction-monitoring and sanctions-screening remediation, and data-governance programmes; read-across work for peer banks on correspondent-banking controls.
bigMoves.body: The U.S. Treasury announced penalties of more than $1.21 billion against Bank of America from FinCEN, the OCC and OFAC.
paras: The U.S. Treasury announced on 13 October 2026 penalties of more than $1.21 billion against Bank of America: $1.2 billion from FinCEN, a $750 million civil penalty from the OCC and an $11.6 million OFAC settlement. According to Treasury, the bank admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act and failed to timely report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, with the OCC saying failures continued after a December 2024 cease-and-desist order.

Treasury says the FinCEN consent order requires a third-party lookback and independent reviews of monitoring, customer due diligence, foreign correspondent due diligence and data governance. OFAC cited 475 apparent sanctions violations. Al Jazeera reports that the OCC fine is the largest in its history and that Bank of America said it is responsible for getting financial crime compliance right and is working to address the issues. The conduct described is as alleged by the regulators and partly admitted in the FinCEN order.
unknowns: Cost and timeline of the required lookback were not disclosed
Whether other regulators or private claims will follow was not reported

bigMoves.vlabel: Italian privacy fine; Meta to appeal
bigMoves.title: Italy's privacy regulator fines Meta EUR 805 million over Facebook's Android photo-gallery feature
bigMoves.cs: Consent-flow and permission-design reviews, privacy-by-default audits of app features, and regulatory-strategy work on which EU authority has jurisdiction over big platforms.
bigMoves.body: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta EUR 805 million over a Facebook feature that accessed Android users' photo galleries, according to TechRepublic.
paras: Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, announced on 14 November 2026 a EUR 805 million ($887 million) fine on Meta, according to TechRepublic and CyberInsider. The regulator found Facebook did not clearly explain, or obtain specific consent for, a gallery-suggestion feature that was on by default and affected about 20 million Android users, the outlets report.

According to CyberInsider, the Garante found a violation of Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code and ordered Meta to switch the feature off by default and seek separate consent within 60 days. Meta disputes the decision and plans to appeal, the outlets say; TechRepublic reports it argued that Ireland's regulator should handle the case, which Italy rejected, and CyberInsider quotes it calling the fine disproportionate. TechRepublic adds that the regulator denied that the material was used for AI training. The findings are the regulator's; Meta contests them.
unknowns: Appeal outcome and any stay of the 60-day compliance order
Whether other EU regulators will examine the same feature

bigMoves.vlabel: Share fall over four days cited in complaint
bigMoves.title: Alibaba is sued by shareholders over alleged under-disclosure of export-control risk tied to Megaspeed
bigMoves.cs: Export-control and sanctions compliance reviews, third-party and customer due-diligence programmes, and risk-disclosure advice for firms buying or reselling advanced AI compute.
bigMoves.body: A shareholder filed a proposed class action in Manhattan federal court alleging Alibaba understated export-control risk, according to the Manila Times.
paras: A shareholder filed a proposed class action on 19 November 2026 in federal court in Manhattan against Alibaba, alleging it inflated its share price by understating, in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports, the risk that actual or suspected export-control violations could harm its business, according to the Manila Times. The suit covers buyers of Alibaba's ADSs from 23 May 2024 to 11 November 2026 and seeks unspecified damages. FourWeekMBA reports that CEO Eddie Wu is also named.

The complaint points to Alibaba's reported ties to Megaspeed, a Singapore company suspected of helping Beijing access advanced Nvidia chips, including reports that Alibaba became its dominant customer, the outlet says. Alibaba shares fell 14% over four days, partly after a 12 November Reuters report on possible tighter U.S. limits on remote chip use. FourWeekMBA says lead-plaintiff motions are due by 19 January 2027. These are allegations; no court has ruled, and Alibaba had not responded when the outlets published.
unknowns: Alibaba's response to the allegations was not reported
Neither outlet read the complaint; details come from Reuters and the plaintiffs' law firm

bigMoves.vlabel: Works at issue in the Canadian suit
bigMoves.title: Ontario appeal court lets Canadian publishers' copyright suit against OpenAI proceed
bigMoves.cs: AI training-data provenance and licensing audits, jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction legal-risk mapping for model developers, and content-licensing strategy for publishers.
bigMoves.body: The Ontario Court of Appeal dismissed OpenAI's appeal, so a copyright suit by Canadian news organisations can proceed in Ontario, according to BNN Bloomberg.
paras: The Ontario Court of Appeal dismissed OpenAI's appeal on 13 November 2026, allowing a copyright lawsuit by Canadian news organisations to proceed in Ontario, according to BNN Bloomberg and Tech Times. The plaintiffs include The Canadian Press, Torstar, The Globe and Mail, Postmedia and CBC/Radio-Canada, and they allege OpenAI used their content to train ChatGPT without permission or payment.

OpenAI had argued the case belonged in a U.S. court, BNN Bloomberg reports; the appeal court found no evidence that a Canadian judgment would conflict with U.S. law. Tech Times says the panel found a real and substantial connection to Ontario, and that the case will be judged under Canadian law, which has no text-and-data-mining exception like U.S. fair use. The ruling decides venue only, not infringement; Tech Times reports the plaintiffs seek statutory damages of up to $20,000 per work across 10.65 million works, and that OpenAI may seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The claims are unproven.
unknowns: Whether OpenAI will seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada
Whether training copying occurred in Canada, which could affect liability

bigMoves.title: Sonoco names insider Ernest Haynes to succeed retiring CEO Howard Coker
bigMoves.cs: Leadership-transition support, 100-day planning and portfolio review for a new CEO at a packaging group refocused on consumer and industrial segments.
bigMoves.body: Sonoco said on 9 November that CEO Howard Coker will retire and Ernest Haynes III, head of its global consumer packaging business, has been elected to succeed him.
paras: According to Sonoco's release, R. Howard Coker, CEO since 2020 and a 41-year company veteran, will stay in the role through 31 December 2026. Ernest D. Haynes III, president of Global Consumer Packaging since August 2026, succeeds him as president, CEO and director. Chairman John Haley described the change as the result of a planned succession process, per the release.

Haynes joined Sonoco in 1997 and has held roles across both its Consumer and Industrial segments, including leading metal and rigid paper packaging through the integration of major acquisitions, the company says. Paper Age carried the same announcement. Sonoco reported $7.5 billion of 2025 sales from continuing operations and has about 22,000 employees, according to the release.

The handover comes as Sonoco presents itself as a more focused business built around consumer and industrial packaging, which makes the new CEO's portfolio and capital-allocation choices the thing to watch.
unknowns: Haynes's strategic priorities and any portfolio changes were not set out in the release
Whether the succession is accompanied by other executive changes was not stated

bigMoves.vlabel: CFO Leibrock steps in as CEO Warsop leaves
bigMoves.title: ACI Worldwide CEO Thomas Warsop quits for another public company; CFO named interim
bigMoves.cs: CEO search and succession advisory, interim-leadership governance and strategy reviews for a payments software vendor with falling profit and a pending acquisition.
bigMoves.body: ACI Worldwide said CEO Thomas Warsop has stepped down to run another public company and named CFO Robert Leibrock interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.
paras: According to the announcement carried by MarketScreener, Warsop left as CEO effective 18 November 2026 after accepting a CEO post at a public company in a different industry, and will remain with ACI until 18 December to support the transition. CFO Robert Leibrock, who joined in July 2025 after senior finance roles at Red Hat, becomes interim CEO. The board has hired a search firm and will consider internal and external candidates.

Payments Dive reports an SEC filing says there was no disagreement behind the resignation, that ACI reaffirmed the guidance issued with its third-quarter results, and that Warsop took over in 2023 after the abrupt exit of his predecessor. It also notes net income for the first nine months fell 37% to $102.6 million.
MarketScreener's page shows the shares closing at $50.50 on 19 November, down 4.5% that day; the page does not attribute the move to the leadership change.
unknowns: Which company Warsop is joining was not disclosed
Whether Leibrock is a candidate for the permanent role is not stated

bigMoves.title: Cooper Companies replaces CEO Al White with executive chair Walt Rosebrough after Jana pressure
bigMoves.cs: Board refresh and CEO search support, portfolio review of CooperVision versus surgical assets, and turnaround planning for a medtech company under activist pressure.
bigMoves.body: Cooper Companies replaced CEO Albert White with board member Walter Rosebrough as executive chair, weeks after activist Jana Partners urged a CEO search and a look at asset sales, according to MedTech Dive.
paras: According to MedTech Dive, Albert White stepped down as president and CEO effective immediately after eight years in the role and will advise through April. Walter Rosebrough Jr., a director and former Steris CEO, becomes executive chair and runs day-to-day operations until a permanent CEO is named, with Russell Reynolds supporting the search. A new independent director joins in December and three directors will not stand for re-election in 2027.

MedTech Dive says Jana Partners had demanded in September that Cooper start an external CEO search, appoint a new chair, consider selling its fertility and medical device assets and engage with buyers for CooperVision. Finimize reports Cooper reaffirmed its fiscal 2026 outlook and that its shares fell almost 3% in extended trading.
Note that the announcement was on 27 October, slightly before this week's window, but the follow-through on the search and any asset review is still ahead.
unknowns: Jana's stake size was not disclosed in the coverage read
Whether the board will pursue the asset sales Jana asked for is unclear

bigMoves.vlabel: Cut since June; Elevate savings target $1B
bigMoves.title: Fiserv discloses 3,000 job cuts and doubles Project Elevate savings target to $1 billion
bigMoves.cs: Operating-model redesign, AI-enabled cost take-out, product-portfolio rationalisation and management-layer reductions at a payments processor under activist scrutiny.
bigMoves.body: Fiserv said on its third-quarter call that it has cut about 3,000 employee and contractor roles since June and raised its Project Elevate savings target to $1 billion from $500 million.
paras: According to People Matters, Fiserv disclosed on 3 November that roughly 3,000 employee and contractor positions have gone since June and that senior management was reduced by more than 10%. The company had more than 38,000 employees at the end of 2025, per the same report. AI Weekly, citing PYMNTS, says management framed the programme as an AI-everywhere reorganisation, with fraud review, customer service and software work slated for automation.

Fiserv's results release confirms the Project Elevate target rose to $1 billion from $500 million after a portfolio review, and reports $83 million of severance in the quarter plus a $6.45 billion goodwill impairment. People Matters reports Fiserv also plans to exit more than a dozen smaller products and that the new target sits below the $1.25 billion activist Jana Partners had proposed; the release itself did not mention product exits.
Both trade outlets report shares rising about 9.5% premarket.
unknowns: Which divisions bore the cuts and the period for the $1B savings were not disclosed
The results release gave no headcount figures; the 3,000 figure comes from the call as reported

bigMoves.vlabel: About 15% of KLM workforce; EUR 1B uplift
bigMoves.title: KLM to cut, outsource or transfer about 5,000 jobs in cost-reset drive
bigMoves.cs: Airline cost-base redesign, outsourcing and shared-services strategy, fleet and productivity programmes, and union-facing transformation planning.
bigMoves.body: KLM said it will remove about 5,000 jobs, nearly 15% of its workforce, through cuts, outsourcing and transfers to its parent, with CEO Marjan Rintel warning the airline's future is not guaranteed.
paras: Announced on 5 November alongside Air France-KLM's third-quarter results, the plan covers about 5,000 positions, according to DutchNews.nl and Skift. Skift breaks it down as roughly 1,250 catering jobs moved to Gategroup, 800 ground-services roles shifted to third parties, 2,000 positions transferred to Air France-KLM (1,500 at contact centre Cygnific) and about 1,000 reductions from productivity gains.

Skift reports KLM is targeting an extra EUR 1 billion a year of earnings improvement, taking the total to EUR 1.4 billion, and is seeking union agreement to an 8% productivity gain by 2028 with restrained wages. DutchNews.nl says KLM expects to avoid compulsory layoffs, relying on voluntary schemes and unfilled vacancies, and that unions FNV and CNV have voiced concern.
The cuts come despite a stronger quarter: Skift reports KLM's operating profit rose to EUR 458 million.
unknowns: Implementation timetable and the final number of outright redundancies were not given
Union response and negotiation outcome remain open

bigMoves.vlabel: European net cuts; five sites to close
bigMoves.title: Schaeffler to cut 3,460 European jobs and close five sites
bigMoves.cs: Footprint and capacity consolidation, spans-and-layers redesign, and EV-versus-combustion portfolio strategy for an automotive supplier.
bigMoves.body: Schaeffler said it will cut a net 3,460 jobs across 16 European sites and close five locations, aiming for about EUR 300 million of annual earnings improvement.
paras: According to Evertiq, Schaeffler announced the programme on 3 November with its third-quarter results: a net 3,460 positions go in Europe, about 2,660 of them in Germany, across 16 sites, with five sites closing over time, four in Germany. Named closures include Dortmund, Morbach and Berlin, and Schwalbach is also affected, Evertiq reports. Roughly half the roles are in production and 30% in R&D.

Evertiq reports earnings should improve by about EUR 300 million a year from 2030 against one-off costs of about EUR 480 million, with implementation mainly in 2027 and 2028. electrive says Schaeffler blames weak combustion-engine demand, slower electric-mobility growth and high German labour costs, and that e-mobility lost EUR 571 million in nine months.
electrive also cites Handelsblatt as saying at least two of seven management levels below the board will be removed and the executive board will shrink to eight.
unknowns: Social-plan and works-council negotiations were not reported as concluded
The count is net; gross reductions were not stated

bigMoves.title: UGI plans to spin off its global LPG business, separating from its regulated utilities
bigMoves.cs: Separation planning, Form 10 and capital-structure design, TSA and stand-alone cost work, and valuation advice as an energy group splits propane from utilities.
bigMoves.body: UGI's board approved a plan to spin off its global LPG business, combining UGI International and AmeriGas Propane, with completion targeted for the second half of 2027.
paras: According to UGI's release of 18 November, the new LPG company would be the largest publicly listed LPG distributor in the world and the largest US retail propane distributor, while New UGI keeps regulated gas utilities in Pennsylvania and West Virginia plus midstream assets. Shareholders would receive LPG shares pro rata in a transaction intended to be tax-free, and New UGI may retain up to 19.9% initially. J.P. Morgan and Latham & Watkins are advising.

The Philadelphia Inquirer reports UGI shares fell 8% on 19 November to $35.18, nearly erasing the gain from a KKR approach in August at $42.50 a share, and that CEO Bob Flexon said he is not completely opposed to selling the whole company for a better offer.
The release says final board approval, an effective Form 10 and debt consents are required and that there is no assurance the separation will occur.
unknowns: Leadership, capital structure and dividend policy for each company are to be detailed later
Whether a whole-company bid re-emerges is unclear

bigMoves.title: Kraft Heinz sells North American coffee business to One Rock Capital for $650 million
bigMoves.cs: Carve-out, TSA and stranded-cost work for the coffee unit, plus portfolio-focus and supply-chain consolidation support for Kraft Heinz.
bigMoves.body: Kraft Heinz agreed to sell its North American coffee business, including Maxwell House and Gevalia, to private equity firm One Rock Capital Partners at a $650 million enterprise value.
paras: According to Bloomberg Law, the deal values the unit at $650 million, with Kraft Heinz retaining a 30% non-controlling stake and closing expected in mid-2027. ConsumerGoods.com lists the brands as Maxwell House, Gevalia, Nabob, Yuban, Tassimo, Ethical Bean and Sanka, with about 250 full-time employees and plants in Jacksonville and Vancouver expected to transfer.

ConsumerGoods.com reports Kraft Heinz expects net proceeds of about $500 million to pay down debt and that CEO Steve Cahillane called it a step in unlocking portfolio value. Bloomberg Law says the sale narrows the portfolio as the company seeks to restart growth.
ConsumerGoods.com adds the move sits within a wider restructuring that includes consolidating supply-chain functions and a shift away from a planned company split.
unknowns: Kraft Heinz's own release was not read; terms are as reported by outlets
Employee and plant transfer details beyond the reported figures were not given

bigMoves.title: Sylvamo proposes sale of its Europe paper business to Midas Atlantic Partners
bigMoves.cs: Carve-out and separation planning, works-council consultation process support and post-sale refocus on Latin America and North America.
bigMoves.body: Sylvamo has entered a put option agreement for the sale of its Europe business to Midas Atlantic Partners with The Najafi Companies, with closing targeted by the end of Q1 2027.
paras: According to Sylvamo's 6 November release, the proposed sale covers its uncoated freesheet mills in Saillat, France and Nymolla, Sweden, plus forestry and supporting operations. The buyer would take the business with an agreed level of working capital and cash, and Sylvamo would keep the right to 20% of future distributions. A definitive share purchase agreement follows works-council consultation.

The release quotes CEO John Sims describing it as an important strategic step that will leave Sylvamo more focused. Finviz's earnings coverage reports the European business is already shown as discontinued operations and that shares rose about 12% on the day.

howItWorks.title: How Canadian telecom makes money
howItWorks.body: Rogers, Bell and Telus together turned about 42.5 cents of each revenue dollar into adjusted EBITDA in Q3 2026 (computed), because the network is built once and rented every month. But average revenue per phone fell at Rogers and Bell, and the CRTC is pushing prices and fees lower, so growth now depends on churn and cost control.
howItWorks.summary: The Big Three earned about C$7.1 billion of adjusted EBITDA on C$16.6 billion of revenue in Q3 2026 (computed). Here is how wireless ARPU, churn, spectrum, capex and CRTC rules decide who keeps the margin.
howItWorks.ai: AI is mainly a capital-spending story for Bell, which names its AI data centre build-out as a driver of a 49.3% jump in capex, and a cost-cutting story for Telus, which targets about C$900 million of annual savings by 2028. None of the releases quantifies AI savings, so treat any such claim as unproven.
howItWorks.caseq: A national wireless carrier's service revenue is down 1% and ARPU is down 2.6%, yet postpaid churn is 1.03% and net additions have collapsed from 62,000 to 6,000. A challenger is adding lines fast. The CEO asks whether to cut prices to win customers back. What do you recommend?
howItWorks.caseAnswer: Frame wireless profit as subscribers x ARPU x margin, less the cost of replacing churned customers, then test each driver. 1) Diagnose the ARPU fall: separate regulatory fee loss (the CRTC fee ban, which carriers say cut fee revenue) from true price competition and from mix (more low-price or prepaid lines). Fee loss is not winnable with price cuts. 2) Test churn economics: at about 1% a month, roughly one subscriber in nine leaves each year (computed), so even a small churn gain is worth more than a gross-add price war; compare the cost of acquiring a customer with the lifetime margin on one. 3) Check the margin cushion: Rogers earned a 68% EBITDA margin on wireless service revenue even with falling revenue, so there is room to invest, but not to cut price across the whole base, which would reprice customers who were not leaving. 4) Choose targeted levers: price-match offers for at-risk customers, bundles with home internet to cut churn, and higher-priced plans for new customers (the finance chief says new-customer ARPU is up 8%). 5) Watch the competitors and the regulator: wholesale MVNO access and a fee review can change the field, so scenario-test both. Recommend a targeted retention and bundling approach, funded by cost cuts, rather than a blanket price cut, with metrics reviewed monthly: churn, ARPU by cohort, net adds and EBITDA margin.
cheat: Rogers Q3 2026: revenue C$5,443M, adjusted EBITDA C$2,535M, wireless service margin 68.0%, ARPU C$55.22, postpaid churn 1.03% (Rogers Q3 2026 release, SEC 6-K).
BCE Q3 2026: revenue C$6,182M, adjusted EBITDA C$2,786M (45.1% margin), mobile phone ARPU C$57.07, capex C$1,330M (BCE Q3 2026 results via TelecomTV; BCE MD&A, SEC 6-K).

Telus Q3 2026: revenue C$5,020M, adjusted EBITDA C$1,760M, ARPU C$57.22, churn 1.01%, 84,000 mobile phone net additions, net loss C$660M after an C$800M TELUS Health impairment (Telus Q3 2026 release, SEC 6-K).
Big Three combined Q3 2026: revenue C$16,645M, adjusted EBITDA C$7,081M, margin about 42.5% (computed from the three releases).

CRTC: 2024 telecom revenue C$59.6B, mobile C$33.6B (56.4%); the three largest operators hold about 90% of wireless and over 90% of wireless EBITDA (CRTC Canadian Telecommunications Market Report 2026).
CRTC: new competitors took over 55% of mobile net additions in 2024; mobile ARPU about C$68.41 with devices, about C$51 without (CRTC market report 2026).
MVNO: Policy 2021-130 set a seven-year mandated wholesale access period for eligible regional carriers on Bell, Rogers, Telus and SaskTel networks (CRTC MVNO page).
Spectrum: the 2021 3500 MHz auction raised C$8.91B; Rogers' release says the mmWave auction moved to January 25, 2028 (ISED; Rogers Q3 2026 release).
