howItWorks.cs: Carriers face falling revenue per user, fee rules under CRTC review and a fresh capex cycle in fibre and AI infrastructure, so they need cost, pricing and churn analysis. Investors and B.C. employers following Telus will want scenarios on its efficiency plan and leverage target.

paras: A Canadian phone and internet company is a toll collector on a network it had to build first. It pays up front for towers, fibre and radio spectrum, then rents access to households and businesses by the month. The profit comes from how many people pay, how much each pays, and how few leave, set against a bill for equipment that never stops growing.

The three big carriers are large and highly profitable on paper. In the third quarter of 2026, Rogers reported revenue of C$5,443 million and adjusted EBITDA of C$2,535 million, BCE reported C$6,182 million and C$2,786 million, and Telus reported C$5,020 million and C$1,760 million. Added together, that is C$16,645 million of revenue and C$7,081 million of adjusted EBITDA, a combined margin of about 42.5% (computed). The companies define and mix their segments differently, so the total is a rough scale rather than a clean comparison.

The structure is tight. The CRTC's 2026 market report, which covers 2024, puts Canadian telecom revenue at C$59.6 billion, of which mobile was C$33.6 billion, or 56.4%. It says the three largest operators hold about 90% of the national wireless market and account for over 90% of wireless EBITDA.

The quarter's theme was slowing growth. Rogers added only 6,000 postpaid phone customers against 62,000 a year earlier, and its chief executive estimated that industry-wide wireless net additions fell 30 to 40%, according to a trade report on the call. When the market stops adding people quickly, carriers have to win on price, retention and cost, and that is where the money gets made or lost.

There are three engines. The first is wireless: a monthly plan multiplied by the number of subscribers, plus phones sold through the carrier. Rogers' wireless segment earned C$2,033 million of service revenue and C$655 million of equipment revenue in the quarter. Bell's wireless service revenue was C$1,781 million, down 1.3%, and Telus' consolidated service revenue was about C$4.5 billion, down 1%.

The second engine is the fixed network: home internet, TV and phone over cable or fibre. Rogers' cable arm earned C$1,987 million of revenue at a 58.6% margin, with 4,531,000 retail internet subscribers and 10,000 net additions, down from 29,000. Bell reported 3,697,621 residential fibre-to-the-home subscribers, up 2.8%, while its total high-speed internet base fell 2.1% to 4,942,447. Cable video and home phone are shrinking, since Rogers lost about 110,000 video and 114,000 home phone subscribers in a year (computed from 2,414K vs 2,524K and 1,307K vs 1,421K).

The third engine is everything else: media, business services and, increasingly, adjacent bets. Rogers' media arm, which includes Sportsnet, earned C$821 million at a 10.2% margin. Bell Media earned C$803 million, and Bell's business unit reported revenue up 9.2% with AI-powered solutions revenue up 41%. Telus runs a health arm and a digital services arm; the quarter included a C$800 million non-cash impairment on Telus Health, which turned a profit line into a net loss of C$660 million.

The price per customer is the headline unit. Mobile phone ARPU, the average monthly revenue per user, was C$57.22 at Telus (flat), C$57.07 at Bell (down 1.7%) and C$55.22 at Rogers (down 2.6%, from C$56.70). Two of the three cite the CRTC's ban on certain activation and modification fees as part of the fall. Rogers' finance chief said customers added in Q3 and October carry ARPU about 8% higher than a year ago, which suggests the pricing floor may be stabilising, though that is management's claim.

Start with cost structure. BCE's operating costs were C$3,396 million on C$6,182 million of revenue, about 54.9% of revenue (computed), which leaves its 45.1% EBITDA margin. Rogers' is 46.6%; Telus' is about 35.1% (computed), lower because it carries the thinner-margin digital services business, whose adjusted EBITDA was C$62 million on C$637 million of revenue, roughly 9.7% (computed). BCE's release does not give a labour-versus-other split in the text I read, so I will not guess one. The signal on labour is in the cuts: Rogers booked C$104 million of restructuring, mostly severance, in the quarter, and BCE said Bell Canada's costs fell because of workforce reductions.

The margin is high because the marginal customer costs little once the network exists. Rogers' wireless segment earned a 68.0% margin on service revenue (up from 66.7%) even as service revenue fell 1%. Wireless produced C$1,383 million of Rogers' C$2,535 million consolidated EBITDA, about 55% (computed), so the wireless profit pool dominates, followed by cable, with media a small contributor.

What eats the cash is capital spending. Bell spent C$1,330 million in the quarter, 21.5% of revenue, up 49.3%, with its AI data centre build-out and its U.S. fibre business as stated drivers. Telus spent C$701 million, about 14.0% of revenue (computed), and guides to roughly C$2.6 billion for the year. Rogers spent C$524 million, down 46%, about 9.6% of revenue (computed); the release text I read did not explain the timing. Together the three spent C$2,555 million, about 36% of their combined EBITDA (computed).

Debt makes the margin a smaller prize. Rogers' leverage ratio was 3.7 times at quarter-end, down from 4.0 at December 2025, and Telus' net debt was 3.6 times EBITDA against a target of 3.0 or lower by the end of 2028. Rogers' free cash flow rose 65% to C$1,370 million, partly because capex fell, and it then paid C$4.35 billion in cash on October 1 for the remaining stake in MLSE, funded from credit facilities.

The cycle behaviour is defensive. People keep their phone and internet in a downturn, and the CRTC counts telecom revenue as flat in 2024. The swing factors are net additions, promotions and regulation, not the business cycle.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: The number is the product of three figures: subscribers, ARPU and churn. Churn is the share of subscribers who leave each month. Postpaid churn was 1.01% at Telus (a three-year low), 1.03% at Rogers (up from 0.99%) and 1.06% at Bell (down 7 basis points). A monthly rate near 1% sounds trivial, but compounded over twelve months it means roughly one subscriber in nine leaves each year (computed), and each one has to be replaced by marketing, discounts and handset subsidies before the base grows at all.

This is why a carrier will accept a lower ARPU to keep a customer. Prepaid is the extreme: churn was 4.77% at Rogers (from 2.86%) and 5.32% at Bell (from 5.10%), which makes prepaid a high-turnover, low-loyalty product.

Here is the counter-intuitive fact. Telus won the quarter on subscribers, with 84,000 net phone additions against Bell's 24,000 postpaid and Rogers' 6,000, yet its adjusted EBITDA fell 5%. Rogers added the fewest customers and its EBITDA rose 1%, because a bigger share of each service dollar was kept. In this industry, who grows the fastest is not the same as who earns the most; cost control and ARPU decide it. Trade press adds that Quebecor, which owns Freedom, Fizz and Videotron, added nearly 137,000 lines, the fastest of any carrier.

ARPU is also where the regulator touches earnings most directly. The CRTC report puts 2024 mobile ARPU at about C$68.41 including devices and about C$51 excluding them, both lower than in 2023. Falling ARPU is a multi-year trend, not a one-quarter event.

AI shows up in these filings as a growth bet first and a cost saver second. Bell's AI Fabric data centre programme is named as a driver of its capex jump, and BCE announced a non-binding memorandum for up to 900 MW of further capacity in Saskatchewan. Bell's AI-powered solutions revenue grew 41%. Telus says it intends to become a leading communications and AI infrastructure player in Canada.

On costs, the evidence is thinner. BCE credits technology and automation-enabled operating efficiencies for part of the cost reduction at Bell Canada but also says AI-powered solutions growth raises costs, and it gives no figure for AI savings. Severance was C$11 million in the quarter and C$59 million year to date, against C$250 million over the same nine months of 2025. Telus targets about C$900 million of annualised cash savings exiting 2028, around 80% from core telecom, and raised its 2026 restructuring cost assumption to about C$900 million from about C$500 million. The release does not say how much of this is AI.

My read, as analysis: AI helps most in customer care, network operations and billing, which are large cost lines, but its effect is invisible in revenue per user. The bigger strategic question is whether AI traffic and data centres become a new profit pool for network owners, or just another capex programme with uncertain returns. Bell's capex intensity of 21.5% is the early cost of that bet.

The regulator sets the edges. The CRTC's Policy 2026-43, issued March 12, 2026, prohibits certain activation and modification fees, and on June 30 it asked Rogers, Bell and Telus to show cause on other fees. For wholesale, a decision finalised rates for some high-speed internet services and required an aggregated wholesale fibre service, and Bell's release says a retroactive effect hurt its Q2 wireline revenue. For wireless, regional carriers with their own spectrum can use the big networks under a seven-year mandated MVNO access arrangement set in Policy 2021-130, with rates negotiated or settled by final-offer arbitration. The CRTC says new competitors took over 55% of mobile net additions in 2024, which shows the wholesale route is being used.

Spectrum is the other gate. Canada's 3500 MHz auction in 2021 raised C$8.91 billion in total. The next mmWave auction was pushed from October 19, 2027 to January 25, 2028, according to Rogers' release, and Telus paid more than C$53 million in spectrum renewal fees to ISED in the first nine months of 2026. Spectrum is a licence, so it is a durable moat, but it is also a recurring bill.

For British Columbia, Telus is the local reference point: its releases are datelined Vancouver, and its C$900 million efficiency plan, C$2.6 billion capex guide and C$0.1875 quarterly dividend all matter to its investors and to anyone who works with a Vancouver-headquartered carrier. The release does not give a B.C. split or say where jobs will fall, so I will not guess.

So who wins? The carrier with the lowest churn and the lowest cost per connection, which can keep ARPU from falling while it pays down debt. Telus has the best churn this quarter but the weakest earnings. Rogers has the healthiest margin and cash flow but is adding the fewest subscribers and now carries a bigger sports bill. Bell is spending the most for a future in fibre and AI data centres. None of the three has solved slower growth, and the CRTC is still pushing prices lower.

howItWorks.title: How Canadian Tire works
howItWorks.body: Canadian Tire reported retail sales of $4.74 billion in the third quarter of 2026, yet in 2025 its credit-card bank earned $334.7 million before tax, against $453.2 million for a retail network that sold nearly $19 billion of goods. The company is part retailer, part bank, part landlord, and the parts feed one another.
howItWorks.summary: Canadian Tire is a retailer with a bank and a landlord attached. Financial Services earned $334.7 million before tax in 2025 against $453.2 million for the whole Retail segment, and CT REIT collects rent from the stores. Here is how dealers, Triangle Rewards, owned brands and credit receivables fit together, and what could break it.
howItWorks.ai: AI is already in the pricing engine: Canadian Tire's DaiVID tool optimises pricing and margin, and management says the Mosaic customer-data platform shapes assortment and marketing. Savings are being reinvested in AI rather than banked, and the company is building a store-operations platform with Microsoft and its dealers.
howItWorks.caseq: A national retailer sells through independent dealers, owns a bank that issues a store credit card, and controls a REIT that owns most of its store land. Tariffs and weak consumer confidence are squeezing retail margin. Where should management invest, and what would you watch?
howItWorks.caseAnswer: Frame the group as four profit pools that share one customer: retail margin, credit-card income, rent and loyalty-driven traffic. 1) Retail: protect a gross margin of about 35% (excluding petroleum) through owned brands and pricing analytics rather than discounting, and judge store investment by sales per square foot and return on invested capital (11.2% in Q3 2026). 2) Financial Services: grow receivables only while credit metrics hold; watch the net write-off rate (7.2%) and allowance rate, because a credit cycle hits this pool first. 3) Property: treat CT REIT as a stable annuity (92.0% of its space is leased to Canadian Tire) and use it to fund store redevelopment, but remember that rent is a cost to the retail segment. 4) Loyalty and dealers: invest where it raises repeat visits (Triangle penetration was 55.5% of retail sales) and keep dealers profitable, since they are independent operators who must keep stocking shelves. Prioritise by size and speed: first test credit quality, because it is the swing factor in profit; then margin; then expansion. Recommend steady investment in the loyalty-plus-owned-brand core, with credit growth gated by write-off data.

howItWorks.cs: Canadian Tire is a retailer whose profit is shaped by a bank, a landlord and a loyalty scheme. Retailers, banks, REIT investors and private-equity buyers hire consultants to benchmark loyalty economics, credit-card profitability, dealer or franchise contracts and private-label strategy.

paras: Canadian Tire looks like a hardware-and-auto shop, but it is better described as three businesses stacked on one customer base. A retail arm sells through stores run by independent dealers and franchisees. A bank, Canadian Tire Bank, lends to those customers on a credit card. A real-estate trust, CT REIT, owns many of the stores and collects rent. A loyalty scheme, Triangle Rewards, ties the three together.

The latest numbers show the scale. In the quarter ended October 3, 2026, the company reported revenue of $4,324.2 million, retail sales of $4,742.8 million and net income attributable to shareholders of $219.6 million, or $4.27 per diluted share, according to its third-quarter release. For 2025, a 53-week year, revenue was $16,315.5 million and normalized diluted EPS was $13.77, up 18.6%, per the fourth-quarter release.

The master question is where the profit actually comes from. The answer is less obvious than the shopfront. In 2025 the Retail segment earned $453.2 million before tax, or $683.7 million on a normalized basis, while Financial Services earned $334.7 million. Add the two reported figures and the bank is about 42% of the total (computed); using the normalized retail figure it is about 33% (computed). If the company stopped selling any single product, little would change. If the credit card or the loyalty scheme stopped working, the company would look quite different.

Run the 60-second test. Who pays? Shoppers at the till, cardholders through interest and fees, and tenants (mostly Canadian Tire itself) through rent. Is revenue recurring? The card balances and rent are; retail sales are repeat but seasonal. Is there a locked-in consumable? Not in the strict sense, but the loyalty money and the card behave like one. Who owns the assets? Mixed: dealers run stores, CT REIT owns property, and the bank carries receivables. What would break it? A credit downturn, a weak consumer, or dealers losing money.

Canadian Tire has at least five engines. The first is selling goods to its network. The annual report says revenue from the sale of goods includes merchandise sold to Dealers, Mark's, SportChek and Party City franchisees, recognised when the goods are delivered, and that a substantial portion of the company's revenue comes from sales to Dealers. In other words, the company is partly a wholesaler to independent operators, not only a shopkeeper. Its corporate website says the Canadian Tire network of about 500 retail operations is managed by third-party operators it calls Dealers.

The second engine is the banner portfolio. At the end of 2025 there were 1,690 retail locations: 673 in the Canadian Tire group (including 171 other-banner stores such as PartSource, PHL and Party City), 354 SportChek, 386 Mark's and 277 gas bars, according to the annual report. Party City in Canada is operated under the Party City name as part of Canadian Tire Retail. Helly Hansen, the outdoor-apparel brand, is no longer part of the story: it was sold to Kontoor Brands on May 31, 2025 for gross proceeds of $1,313.4 million and is shown as discontinued operations.

The third engine is Financial Services. Canadian Tire Bank issues the credit cards and earns interest and fees. The 2025 annual report shows segment revenue of $1,593.8 million, income before tax of $334.7 million, and gross credit-card receivables of $7,555.9 million. The bank funds itself partly from deposits: $2,957.5 million of broker GIC deposits and $584.6 million of retail deposits at year-end. The annual report passages we read did not name a Triangle Mastercard, so we describe it only as the company's credit-card offering.

The fourth is property. CT REIT is majority-owned (67.9% per the Q3 release) and in 2025 reported property revenue of $604.3 million and net operating income of $478.7 million. The company collects its share through distributions, $39.9 million in Q3 2026 alone, recorded in Retail other income. The fifth engine is the loyalty and owned-brand layer, covered below. Stacking these is the point: a franchise-style wholesale margin, a lending margin, rent and a private-label margin all sit on the same footfall.

Start with retail. Consolidated gross margin in 2025 was $5,615.3 million on revenue of $16,315.5 million, about 34.4% (computed from the annual report). In Q3 2026 the retail gross margin rate excluding petroleum was 35.6%, down 16 basis points, and management's stated long-term anchor is 35% or better. Retail SG&A in the quarter was $784.1 million, up 0.5%, and Retail income before tax was $197.9 million against $144.6 million a year earlier.

Sales per square foot is the trade measure for a store network. SportChek was at $346, up 5.8%, on a rolling 12-month basis in Q3 2026 with 311 stores, down from 319, according to Retail Insider. The pattern is fewer, better stores: SportChek counts fell from 371 to 354 across 2025, while Mark's rose from 383 to 386.

Now the bank. Receivables were $7,555.9 million at the end of 2025. Financial Services income before tax of $334.7 million is about 4.4% of average gross receivables of $7,524 million (computed). That return is large only because the book is high-yielding and risky: the net write-off rate was 7.2% and the allowance rate 12.0% in Q4 2025, according to the annual report. In Q3 2026, income before tax rose to $99.2 million from $84.4 million, with receivables up 4.2% and the allowance unchanged at $935 million, per the earnings call summary on Investing.com. Quarterly Financial Services profit was about 31% of consolidated income before tax of $319.4 million (computed).

Third, the capital. Retail return on invested capital was 11.2% in Q3 2026, up from 10.6%, and the company plans about $2 billion of operating capital investment across 2025 to 2028, with 2026 operating capex of $450 million to $500 million. It spent $442.4 million buying back shares in 2025, and raised the annual dividend to $7.30 from $7.20, its 17th consecutive increase.

A warning on noise: reported 2025 diluted EPS from continuing operations was $10.57 against $14.91, while the normalized figure rose to $13.77 from $11.61. The reported fall reflects items outside the underlying business, so we use normalized figures where the company discloses them and say so.

sections.h: The number that runs the business
paras: If one number must be chosen, it is the share of retail sales that goes through the loyalty programme, 55.5% on a direct-scan basis in 2025, up 112 basis points, according to the annual report. It runs the business because it connects the three profit pools. A shopper who scans Triangle earns Canadian Tire Money, is marketed to with data, is more likely to carry the card and so generates interest, and shops again in a store sitting on CT REIT land.

Triangle had 9.8 million active registered members at the end of 2025, up 6%. Partners are being added: Petro-Canada and RBC are active, WestJet was due in Q2 2026 and Tim Hortons in the second half. In Q3 2026 loyalty sales grew 6.3% against retail sales growth of 4.4%, and about three million unique members were engaged through partners, up from about two million, though only about 15% were linked to more than one partner, according to Retail Insider and management. Management targets four million over time.

The second number to watch is the credit net write-off rate, 7.2% in both Q4 2025 and Q3 2026, because the bank's profit sits on the gap between interest earned and losses. Tariffs and a weak consumer put pressure on exactly this line. Management said on the call that insolvencies were lower than feared, which is encouraging but is a statement, not a guarantee.

A word on private labels. The 2025 annual report gives Owned Brands penetration of 36.5% of Retail sales, a slight dip from 36.7%. Owned brands matter because the company captures the manufacturer margin as well as the retail one, and because shoppers who learn the labels have fewer reasons to compare elsewhere. The sections we read did not name individual brands, so we do not list them.

AI at Canadian Tire is mostly about pricing, assortment and marketing, not about replacing labour on the shop floor. The FY2025 release describes DaiVID, an AI pricing and margin tool, and in-stock optimisation as live. On the Q3 2026 call, management said its modules would reach Mark's and SportChek in Q4, mainly for 2027 value, and that the Mosaic customer-data platform guided the back-to-school programme and informs assortment and marketing.

The company is also building a store-operations AI platform with Microsoft and its dealers, according to the call summary. That matters because dealers, not head office, employ the store staff and hold much of the inventory, so any productivity gain must be sold to them as well as installed. In Q3 corporate inventory rose 6% while dealer inventory fell 1%, a reminder that the two balance sheets move separately.

The release says 2026 savings will be balanced against investments including AI deployment, so savings are not simply flowing to profit. Exposure on the other side is real: AI shopping agents that compare prices across retailers weaken a business built on habit and a loyalty scheme. Financial Services can use AI for underwriting too, but the filings we read gave no figures for any AI-driven saving, so we state none.

The moat is a combination rather than a single wall. Brand and network: more than 1,600 retail and gas outlets and a brand that is almost a household word. Switching costs: Triangle Rewards balances and the card. Scale and cost: owned brands and national buying. Property: CT REIT holds more than 380 properties at 99.5% occupancy, though Canadian Tire is its dominant tenant at 92.0% of gross leasable area and 90.5% of base minimum rent, per the REIT's Q3 release. The REIT is a stable income stream, but it is not independent evidence of demand; it depends on the parent paying rent.

The dealer model is the least visible and most important piece. Dealers are independent operators who contract with the company, buy merchandise from it and finance inventory and fixed assets partly through Franchise Trust, whose average assets were $550.9 million in 2025. Franchise Trust debt is a legal liability of the dealers, so it sits outside the company's capital definition. The company renegotiated its CTR dealer contracts in Q3 2025. Our sources do not give the number of dealers or their compensation formula, so we do not state them. The consultant's point is incentive design: dealers carry local risk, and the head office must keep them profitable enough to keep investing.

The current strategy, called True North, runs from March 2025 for four years. By the end of 2025 it had delivered 52 store projects, a restructuring with roughly $30 million of run-rate savings, and a Hudson's Bay Company brand capsule. Headlines on Q3 2026 show strong comparable sales (3.2% overall, with Automotive on a 25th consecutive quarter of growth at the Canadian Tire banner and SportChek on its ninth), and a headline that the company is putting $200 million behind Mark's new store format, though we did not read the details.

What could break it? First, credit: a sharp rise in unemployment lifts write-offs on a $7.6 billion book. Second, the consumer: management said consumer confidence has dropped sharply and expects value pricing to persist for another 12 to 18 months, and the Q4 started slowly because of warm weather, a reminder of how seasonal the product mix is. Third, margin: tariffs, fuel and transport costs are headwinds into at least the first half of 2027 per management, against a 35% gross-margin anchor. Fourth, dealer health. Fifth, competition from online and mass retailers. On the positive side Q3 2026 net income was $219.6 million against $169.1 million, and retail return on capital is improving.

A business that makes money from selling goods, lending to its own shoppers and renting its own land can survive a weak year in any one of the three, but not a weak year in all three at once, which is what a recession with high unemployment would deliver.

howItWorks.title: Break-even analysis: how many sales before a business stops losing money
howItWorks.body: Break-even analysis splits costs into fixed and variable to find the sales volume at which a business stops losing money. Here is how it works, what it hides, and what it shows about Air Canada's latest quarter.
howItWorks.summary: Fixed versus variable costs, contribution margin, break-even and operating leverage, applied to Air Canada: a record 89.1% load factor in Q3 2026 against a computed break-even near 85.8%, as fuel rose C$906 million and operating margin fell to 3.7%.
howItWorks.ai: AI is good at pulling cost lines from filings, proposing a fixed and variable split, and running sensitivity grids; it cannot judge whether a cost is truly fixed, how rivals will react, or how thin a cushion a board will accept.
howItWorks.caseq: A regional airline fills 85% of its seats and earns a thin profit. Fuel prices jump 40% and the CEO asks whether the airline should cut capacity, raise fares or do nothing. How would you structure the answer?
howItWorks.caseAnswer: Verdict: first find the break-even load factor and the cushion, then choose levers by cost and reversibility. 1) Baseline: split costs into fixed (aircraft, crews, airports) and variable (fuel by flight, catering, fees), and compute contribution per seat and break-even load factor before and after the fuel move. 2) Price: how much of the fuel increase can fares and fees recover, and what does the likely drop in demand do to load factor? 3) Volume and capacity: which routes or flights fall below break-even, and what is saved by cutting them versus the fixed costs that stay? 4) Costs: hedging, fuel efficiency, fleet and schedule changes, with time to impact. 5) Risks and cash: operating leverage, liquidity, and what triggers the next action. Recommend the cheapest reversible mix, such as selective fare increases and trimming the weakest flights, and set a trigger for deeper cuts.

CFI's example: $60 price, $45 variable cost, $240,000 fixed gives 16,000 units, or $960,000 revenue.
Margin of safety = (sales - break-even sales) / sales; degree of operating leverage = contribution margin / operating income (OpenStax).
Air Canada Q3 2026: revenue C$6,984m, operating income C$261m (3.7% margin), load factor 89.1% vs 86.5% (company release).
Air Canada Q3 2026 fuel expense C$2,118m vs C$1,212m; fuel price 148.3 cents per litre vs 88.3 (company release).
Computed break-even load factor: about 85.8% in Q3 2026 vs about 82.2% in Q3 2025, so the cushion fell from about 4.3 to 3.3 points.
About two-thirds of airline operating expenses are fixed (US, 2019; Transportgeography.org); used here only as an assumption.

facts.v: Fixed costs / contribution per unit = break-even volume
Contribution margin · Margin of safety · Operating leverage

howItWorks.cs: Case-interview use: for any 'will this make money?' question, split fixed and variable costs, compute break-even and margin of safety, then test which lever (price, volume, variable or fixed cost) is cheapest.

paras: Every business pays some bills whether or not anyone buys anything, and some bills only when it sells. Break-even analysis separates the two and asks one question: how much must we sell before the first group of bills is covered? Below that level the business loses money; above it, each extra sale adds profit.

Four terms do the work. Fixed costs do not move with volume in the short run: rent, salaried staff, aircraft ownership. Variable costs rise with each unit sold: materials, delivery, card fees. Contribution margin is the selling price minus the variable cost, the slice of each sale left to pay the fixed costs and then to become profit. The break-even point is the sales volume at which total contribution equals total fixed costs. Corporate Finance Institute gives the formulas: break-even units equal fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit, and break-even revenue is that figure times the price, or fixed costs divided by the contribution margin ratio. Its worked example has a $60 price, $45 variable cost and $240,000 of fixed costs, giving a $15 contribution, a 25% ratio and 16,000 units, or $960,000 of revenue.

Two companion ideas matter just as much. The margin of safety is the cushion between actual sales and the break-even level, in other words how far sales can fall before losses begin. Operating leverage describes how sharply profit reacts to a change in sales. OpenStax's managerial accounting text defines the degree of operating leverage as contribution margin divided by operating income, and says a firm with high fixed costs gains more when sales rise and loses faster when they fall. Air Canada's latest quarter, below, shows exactly that.

Start with the cost split, because everything else depends on it. List every cost line and ask what happens to it if volume rises by one unit, one customer or one flight. Costs that do not move belong in fixed. Costs that move belong in variable. Many are neither: a salaried manager is fixed until a second shift is needed, then the cost jumps. Treat these as step costs and note where each assumption holds. Corporate Finance Institute's guide implies, without saying so outright, that the analysis only works if costs can be cleanly split in this way, and that the hardest part is estimating how sales patterns will respond to changes.

Next, define the unit. For a bakery it is a loaf; for a software firm a subscriber-month; for an airline, an available seat-mile flown and filled. The unit must be something that carries one price and one variable cost. If a company sells five products, work out the break-even on a weighted-average contribution margin for the usual sales mix, and state the mix you assumed, because a shift toward the low-margin product moves the break-even even if total sales are unchanged.

Then compute in three steps. First, contribution per unit: price minus variable cost. Second, break-even units: total fixed costs divided by that contribution. Third, translate into revenue and time, for example dividing by expected monthly sales to see how many months to cover a launch cost.

Finally, read the answer against reality. Compare break-even with realistic sales and compute the margin of safety, using OpenStax's definition: the shortfall of sales from break-even divided by sales. Then compute the degree of operating leverage and use it as a sensitivity multiplier: the percentage change in operating income is roughly the leverage figure times the percentage change in sales. Run it up and down.

Air Canada is a good test because an airline is close to a pure fixed-cost machine and, this autumn, was hit by a large shock to its biggest variable cost. All figures are in Canadian dollars from the company's third-quarter 2026 results release unless marked computed or assumption. The release's own outlook was updated on 29 October 2026.

The bare results first. Third-quarter operating revenue was C$6,984 million, against C$5,774 million a year earlier. Operating expenses were C$6,723 million, against C$5,490 million. Operating income was therefore C$261 million, down from C$284 million, an operating margin of 3.7% against 4.9%. Capacity, measured in available seat miles, rose 5.7% to 29,893 million, and traffic, in revenue passenger miles, rose 8.9% to 26,642 million. The passenger load factor, the share of seats filled, rose from 86.5% to 89.1%. Passenger revenue per mile, or yield, rose 11.0% to 23.8 cents.

Airlines use a version of break-even analysis called the break-even load factor: the share of seats that must be filled to cover costs. The airline does not report one in this release, so we compute a rough one. If costs are set by the flying schedule, and revenue scales with seats filled, the break-even load factor is the actual load factor multiplied by the ratio of costs to revenue. For the third quarter of 2026 that is 89.1% times 6,723 over 6,984, or about 85.8% (computed). A year earlier it was 86.5% times 5,490 over 5,774, or about 82.2% (computed). It rests on a strong simplification, namely that cargo and other revenue move in step with passenger traffic and that no cost varies with passengers, so treat it as an indicator and not a reported measure.

Read it as a margin of safety. In 2025 the airline filled 86.5% of seats against a break-even near 82.2%, a cushion of about 4.3 points (computed). In 2026 it filled 89.1% against about 85.8%, a cushion of about 3.3 points (computed). Higher occupancy bought a smaller cushion, because the break-even itself rose by about 3.5 points (computed). That is the story of the quarter: the airline worked its planes harder and still earned less.

The reason is fuel. Aircraft fuel expense was C$2,118 million against C$1,212 million, up C$906 million, and the fuel price per litre was 148.3 cents against 88.3 cents. Fuel was 31.5% of operating expenses against 22.1% a year earlier (computed). Fuel per available seat mile rose from about 4.3 cents to about 7.1 cents (computed). Strip fuel out and the rest of the cost base rose far more slowly, from about 15.1 cents to about 15.4 cents per available seat mile (computed). The nine-month picture is thinner still: operating income of C$163 million on revenue of C$19,035 million, a 0.9% margin against 3.6%, and a load factor of 87.7% against 84.6%. On the same method the nine-month break-even load factor is about 86.9% (computed).

Now add leverage, with a clearly labelled assumption. Transportgeography.org, drawing on United States airline data for 2019, says about two-thirds of airline operating expenses are fixed. Assume, purely for illustration, that the same split applies to Air Canada's quarter (assumption). Then fixed costs are about C$4,482 million and variable costs about C$2,241 million. Contribution is C$4,743 million, a ratio near 68%, and the break-even revenue is about C$6,599 million, a margin of safety of about 5.5% (all computed under that assumption). The degree of operating leverage is 4,743 over 261, about 18 (computed). On those assumptions a 1% fall in sales would cut operating income by roughly 18%. The split is not Air Canada's, but the direction is clear: a few points of lost demand can wipe out a quarter's profit.

The outlook shows the same exposure. Air Canada cut its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to C$2.4 to 2.7 billion from C$2.9 to 3.2 billion, and expects free cash flow of about break-even, plus or minus C$150 million. It blamed higher expected fuel prices. For the fourth quarter it assumes jet fuel at C$1.72 a litre, up from C$1.29, and expects to offset about 70% of the incremental cost, against 100% before. Across the industry, the International Air Transport Association's June 2026 update puts 2026 net profit at US$23.0 billion, a 2.0% margin, against an earlier forecast near US$41 billion, with fuel at 31.4% of costs against 25.4% in 2025 and a passenger load factor forecast of 84.0%.

Break-even analysis becomes useful when it points at levers. There are only four. Raise the price, which lifts contribution on every unit but may cut volume. Cut variable cost per unit. Cut fixed costs. Raise volume. Each lever moves the break-even in a different way and has a different price, and the job of the analyst is to say which is cheapest and most reversible.

Air Canada's quarter shows all four. Price: yield rose 11.0%, so the airline passed a large part of the fuel shock to customers, and load factor rose too, which is unusual. That is a strength of the franchise, and also a limit, since fares cannot be raised indefinitely. Volume: capacity was up 5.7% in the quarter, but management has said the full year will be about 2.75% above 2025, so the volume lever has been used about as far as the schedule allows. Fixed cost: aircraft, crews and airport costs are committed for the season, so the choice is long-term, for instance deferring deliveries or retiring older aircraft. Variable cost: fuel is the obvious target, but it moves with flying, not with passengers. The company's statement that about half of its fourth-quarter fuel needs is exposed to price swings points to hedging and fuel-efficient flying as the realistic levers.

A second use is the go or no-go test on a new venture. Before launching a route, a store or a product line, compute its stand-alone break-even and compare it with a plausible ramp-up. If break-even volume needs a share of the market no competitor has won, the idea is probably a stretch, whatever the strategic story says.
Finally, set a minimum margin of safety and name the trigger that forces action, such as a fuel price or a load factor. A break-even nobody monitors is a slide, not a control.

The first error is a sloppy cost split. Labelling a cost fixed because it is awkward to trace, or variable because it is easy, can shift the answer by large amounts. Fuel is a good illustration. It is the biggest variable cost for an airline, but it varies with flights, not with passengers, so the cost of carrying one more passenger on a flight already scheduled is tiny. Transportgeography.org makes the same point, saying that most costs are fixed and the marginal cost of an extra passenger is very small, which encourages discounting of unsold seats near departure. Analysts who treat fuel as variable per passenger will get the wrong break-even for a single flight.

The second error is treating the model as exact. The classic version assumes one price, a constant variable cost per unit, fixed costs that stay fixed across the whole range and a stable product mix. In practice discounts grow with volume, a second shift adds cost and customers trade down, so check the model at the volume you expect. The airline example carries the same warning. Our break-even load factor ignores the mix of cabins, cargo and routes, and any hedging gains.

Third, ignoring time and cash. Break-even compares revenue and costs in one period. It does not tell you when you recoup the upfront investment, or whether you run out of cash first. Fourth, forgetting that the cushion shrinks quietly. Air Canada's load factor hit a high and its margin of safety still narrowed, because costs rose faster than occupancy. Watch the break-even level as closely as sales.

Last, worshipping a benchmark. The two-thirds fixed-cost share we borrowed from a United States 2019 chart is a reference point, not a fact about Air Canada. Ask for the company's own cost data before relying on it.

AI is well suited to the mechanical parts. It can extract revenue, cost and volume figures from filings into a consistent table, propose a first-pass fixed and variable split, compute break-even, margin of safety and operating leverage, and run sensitivity grids for price, volume and fuel in seconds. It can also flag when load factor, yield or fuel moves the break-even past a set threshold.

It is weak where judgement matters. Whether a cost is truly fixed depends on contracts, labour agreements and how quickly management will act, none of which appears in a ledger. A model will label a cost fixed or variable by its name and report a precise break-even built on a wrong split. It also cannot tell whether a price rise will hold or how competitors will respond. The practical rule is to let automation do the arithmetic and the monitoring, and to have a person own the cost split, the assumptions and the decision.

paras: The Prudential Regulation Authority published its final Basel 3.1 rules in January 2026, and they take effect in the UK on 1 January 2027, according to an explainer by consultancy Gini on Consultancy.uk on 25 November 2026. The start date moved several times, from January 2025 to July 2025, then January 2026, before settling on 2027.

The output floor stops a bank's modelled risk-weighted assets falling below a share of the standardised-approach figure. It starts at 60% on 1 January 2027 and rises to 65% in 2028, 70% in 2029 and 72.5% in 2030, according to Gini. Operational risk moves to one standardised method and internal models for credit valuation adjustment are withdrawn, according to Gini. Market-risk standardised approaches start in January 2027 and the internal-models approach in January 2028. The PRA is also moving remaining capital rules into its Rulebook, including a Strong and Simple regime for small domestic deposit takers, broadly those under £20 billion of assets.

policy.title: EU pushes its toughest AI Act rules back to December 2027
policy.summary: Lawmakers agreed to delay the AI Act's high-risk obligations by about 16 months. The delay changes when companies must spend on compliance, not whether they must comply.
policy.cs: Banks, insurers, HR-tech and health clients get more time, but still need AI inventories, risk classification and governance programmes. Expect work to be re-phased, not cancelled.

paras: The European Union has agreed to postpone the most demanding parts of its AI Act. Under the Digital Omnibus on AI, obligations for high-risk systems that stand alone now apply from 2 December 2027 instead of 2 August 2026. Rules for high-risk AI built into regulated products, such as machinery, move to 2 August 2028, according to law-firm summaries of the agreement.

High-risk systems are the ones used in areas such as hiring, education, credit and insurance, law enforcement, biometrics and critical infrastructure. The delay was justified by missing technical standards and guidance: companies argued they could not comply with rules that did not yet have a rulebook behind them. The European Commission first proposed the change in November 2025, and Parliament and the Council reached a deal in 2026.

The deal is narrower than the headline suggests. Practitioner analysis notes that the bans on certain AI practices (in force since February 2025) and the rules for general-purpose models (since August 2025) were not touched, and that transparency duties in Article 50 still apply from August 2026. The Omnibus mostly streamlines and clarifies the existing text rather than rewriting its risk-based structure.

For clients, the practical point is timing. Teams that use the extra months to build inventories of their AI systems, classify them by risk and set up governance will be ahead of the queue for conformity assessments in 2027. Those that treat the delay as a cancellation will face a compressed deadline later.

policy.title: Canada's AI plan: big spending, no AI law, new privacy and online-safety bills
policy.summary: Ottawa's AI for All strategy leans on privacy reform and online-safety legislation instead of a dedicated AI act, and adds a trusted-AI certification scheme and sovereign data-centre plans.
policy.cs: Canadian clients face privacy and data-governance obligations first, not an AI-specific regime. Demand: privacy programmes, AI governance and assurance, and sovereign-compute strategy.
paras: Prime Minister Mark Carney and AI Minister Evan Solomon launched Canada's national AI strategy, AI for All, on 4 June 2026. It proposes large-scale data centres, a sovereign AI foundation and measures to attract foreign investment into Canadian AI, and a Canada Trusted AI Certification programme to identify trustworthy products in the market.

The notable choice is what it leaves out. Law-firm and commentary analysis agrees that the government does not plan AI-specific regulation. Instead it relies on updating privacy law and bringing back online-safety legislation, a different path from the EU's dedicated AI Act. An earlier federal bill with AI rules, the Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, died with the previous Parliament, and commentators note the government does not appear to intend to reintroduce AI-specific legislation.

Parliament now has a set of related bills. Solomon tabled a long-awaited private-sector privacy bill with stiff fines in June, and the government has also tabled the Safe Social Media Act, which would create a Digital Safety Act. Solomon has said he is confident the bills together will protect children, personal information and privacy.

Critics, including law professor Michael Geist, have called the strategy big on spending but short on the specifics that matter, such as transparency requirements. For Canadian companies the message is to prepare for stronger privacy duties, and to expect certification and procurement rules to shape which AI products public bodies buy.

policy.title: Washington's push to override state AI laws: what the order does and doesn't do
policy.summary: A December 2025 executive order set up a Justice Department task force to challenge state AI laws. The order alone doesn't cancel them, so companies still have to comply with state rules.
policy.cs: Multi-state clients need a compliance plan that works under both outcomes: state rules stay, or a federal standard replaces them. Scenario planning and regulatory monitoring are the work.
paras: On 11 December 2025 President Trump signed an executive order titled Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence. It directs the Attorney General to create an AI Litigation Task Force whose job is to challenge state AI laws, on grounds such as interference with interstate commerce or conflict with federal law. The Commerce Department was told to review state AI laws and refer potentially unlawful provisions to the task force, with a list due in March 2026.

The order also asks White House advisers to draft a legislative proposal for a single federal framework that would override conflicting state laws, while carving out areas such as child safety, data-centre infrastructure and state government use of AI. It singled out Colorado's algorithmic-discrimination law as an early target.

Legal analysts stress the limits. An executive order is not a statute, so on its own it does not displace state law. Until courts invalidate a state rule, companies must keep complying with it. A February 2026 analysis notes that Colorado's AI Act (effective 30 June 2026) and California's frontier-AI transparency law (effective 1 January 2026) were unlikely to be affected in the short term.

The order has drawn criticism from labour groups and from politicians in both parties, and support from some policy analysts who want a single national standard. For clients that operate across states, the practical task is to build compliance that survives either result.

deskNews.summary: The report points to a lack of beds and community care spots that leave admitted patients stuck in emergency departments.
deskNews.cs: Capacity planning, patient-flow and long-term-care investment are the levers. Hospital and provincial clients need whole-system, not ER-only, fixes.
paras: The Canadian Institute for Health Information said on 24 June that long emergency department waits are made worse by a lack of available spots in long-term care and home care, creating a bottleneck for hospital beds. The institute's director of health system analytics said improving ER waits will take solutions that look at the entire health-care system.

A commentary in Canadian Healthcare Technology agrees ED crowding is a system issue but argues the report focuses only on throughput, a process measure that does not explain why the system is failing or whether patient outcomes are improving.

facts.v: Throughput measures do not show outcomes

unknowns: The sources do not give the national wait-time figures.

deskNews.title: Provinces and generic makers extend their pricing agreement to 2028
deskNews.summary: The pCPA and the Canadian Generic Pharmaceutical Association renewed their pricing deal for two years from 1 October 2026.
deskNews.cs: Generic makers and pharmacies get pricing stability. Brand makers and consultants should model tiered-price erosion on new generics.
paras: The pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance, which negotiates for public drug plans, and the Canadian Generic Pharmaceutical Association extended their generic-drug pricing agreement for two years from 1 October 2026. It keeps the pan-Canadian tiered pricing framework and select-molecule pricing.

The generics association says generic makers supplied about 80% of prescriptions dispensed in Canada in 2025. Benefits and Pensions Monitor reports the 2023 renewal set new single-source generics at 75% of the brand reference price, with automatic drops after that.

deskNews.title: B.C. launches national pharmacare coverage for diabetes drugs and menopause therapy
deskNews.summary: The B.C. plan took effect 1 March 2026. Manitoba, P.E.I. and Yukon have signed their own agreements.
deskNews.cs: Pharmacies, insurers and drug makers face a larger public payer for chronic-disease drugs. Private plan design and pricing follow.
paras: The B.C. government said its PharmaCare National Pharmacare Plan launched for residents on 1 March 2026 and covers the full cost of many diabetes medications and menopausal hormone therapy. Lifetimes Canada says Manitoba, P.E.I. and Yukon have also signed agreements and are phasing in their own timelines.

The same explainer notes new Patented Medicine Prices Review Board guidelines took effect on 1 January 2026 and that the CUSMA renegotiation could affect drug spending if intellectual-property protections for brands lengthen.

deskNews.title: Suncor's profit more than doubles and it lifts its buyback by half
deskNews.summary: Net earnings reached $3.8 billion on stronger crude prices and record refined-product sales. Monthly repurchases rise to $750 million.
deskNews.cs: Integrated oil sands and refining shows how much margin sits downstream. Capital-return policy and maintenance execution are the discussion points for boards.
paras: Suncor reported third-quarter 2026 net earnings of $3.814 billion, or $3.27 a share, up from $1.619 billion a year earlier. Adjusted operating earnings were $4.631 billion and adjusted funds from operations $6.705 billion. Net earnings include a $1.080 billion non-cash asset impairment.

Oil sands production was 948,000 barrels a day against 958,300 a year earlier, as extra maintenance at Syncrude offset a record third quarter at Firebag. Refined product sales hit a third-quarter record of 676,900 barrels a day, helped by wider export capacity. OilPrice reports Suncor raised planned monthly buybacks by 50% to $750 million from October and expects $5.5 billion of repurchases in 2026.

deskNews.title: Cenovus passes one million barrels of oil equivalent a day for the first time
deskNews.summary: Record oil sands output and a record downstream margin drove $5.0 billion of adjusted funds flow. It also agreed to buy Athabasca Oil.
deskNews.cs: A low-cost-volume strategy is working while pipelines are tight. Consolidation of oil sands assets continues.
paras: Cenovus reported upstream production of 1,024 thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day in the third quarter, its highest ever and up more than 50,000 from the second quarter, with oil sands production at 833,000 and records at Foster Creek, Christina Lake and Sunrise. Oil sands operating costs fell to $10.23 a barrel. It generated about $5.0 billion of adjusted funds flow and returned $1.9 billion to shareholders.

RBN Energy says the downstream business posted record operating margins of $1.8 billion and that management expects 2026 upstream output near the top of its guidance range. After the quarter, on 5 October, Cenovus announced a cash-and-stock agreement to acquire Athabasca Oil at about $12.00 a share.

deskNews.title: Canada's two big railways both grow revenue 15% in the third quarter, with volumes up 4% at CN and 6% at CPKC
deskNews.summary: Freight demand held up despite tariff noise. CPKC leaned on cross-border and Mexico traffic while CN grew volumes and free cash flow.
deskNews.cs: Rail volumes are a real-economy signal. Shippers should expect continued network competition and rate discipline.
paras: CPKC reported third-quarter revenue of $4.2 billion, up 15%, on a 6% increase in revenue ton-miles, with core adjusted earnings per share of $1.28, up 16%. Reported operating ratio rose 130 basis points to 64.8%, while the core adjusted ratio was 61.9%. Its CEO said the North American network countered macro headwinds.

Railway Age reports CN's third-quarter revenue was C$4.771 billion, up 15%, with revenue ton-miles up 4% and nine-month free cash flow of C$2.918 billion, up 25%. CN still projects low single-digit revenue ton-mile growth for 2026 and mid-to-high single-digit adjusted EPS growth, tracking toward the top of that range.

deskNews.title: Mortgage arrears are rising slowly, concentrated in Toronto and Vancouver, while wider household credit holds up
deskNews.summary: CMHC expects moderate increases through late 2026. CIBC economists say credit quality is surprising on the upside.
deskNews.cs: Lenders can plan for a slow grind, not a cliff. Underwriting, collections and renewal-retention strategies matter most in the two most exposed metro markets.
paras: CMHC's Housing Observer says the national mortgage arrears rate, measured as 90 or more days behind, rose 7 basis points between the third quarter of 2023 and the third quarter of 2025 and remains low by historical standards. Its model, based on Equifax data, expects moderate increases from late 2025 to late 2026, with Toronto and Vancouver the most at risk.

Canadian Mortgage Professional reports CIBC economists wrote that household credit quality is surprising on the upside, with credit scores improving and early-stage delinquencies easing even as serious mortgage arrears climb. Consumer proposals made up 77% of insolvency filings in the third quarter against 60% in 2019. CIBC expects renewal payment increases to ease notably from February 2027.
questions: How exposed are first-time buyers from the pandemic period at first renewal?

unknowns: Forecasts assumed a policy-rate decline by end-2026; the Bank has since raised rates.
